B.learningIntention: I am learning to frame human reproduction as a coordinated control system that supports continuity and variation.
successCriteria: I can connect reproductive structures, gamete production, hormones, and development in one system map.
I can distinguish biological continuity from the sources of genetic variation.
I can turn an observation into a testable reproductive-biology question without asking for personal disclosure.
B.materials: Paper or the Investigation Notebook and the supplied reproduction-system evidence cards.
B.safety: Use fictional or population-level examples. No learner is asked to disclose reproductive history, sex characteristics, gender, sexual activity, fertility, pregnancy, or health information.

warmup.title: One system, several scales
warmup.prompt: List one event that must happen at the cellular scale, one at the organ scale, and one at the whole-body scale for human reproduction to proceed.
warmup.placeholder: Name the three scales and connect the events in a sequence.

sections.label: System purpose
sections.title: Continuity requires coordination
paragraphs: Human reproduction depends on coordinated events rather than one isolated organ. Meiosis produces haploid gametes, reproductive structures support their development and movement, endocrine signals coordinate timing, fertilization combines genetic information, and development changes a single cell into specialized tissues. A disruption at one step can alter later possibilities without implying that one outcome is inevitable.

A system map should therefore show matter, information, timing, and feedback. Arrows represent a defined influence—such as a hormone reaching a target or a gamete moving through a structure—not a vague statement that two things are related.

sections.label: Continuity and variation
sections.title: Reproduction preserves a genome and reshuffles it
paragraphs: DNA replication and chromosome segregation preserve genetic information across cell divisions. Meiosis, independent assortment, crossing over, and random fertilization create new combinations of alleles. Continuity and variation are not opposites: the same chromosome mechanisms that reliably transmit genes also create differences among gametes and offspring.

When explaining variation, distinguish a new allele produced by mutation from a new combination of existing alleles. A family resemblance does not mean genetic identity, and a probability does not guarantee one outcome in a single conception.

sections.label: Control
sections.title: Signals coordinate events through feedback
paragraphs: The hypothalamus, anterior pituitary, gonads, and reproductive tissues communicate through hormones. A hormone is released, transported in blood, binds receptors on responsive cells, and changes target activity. Feedback returns information about the response and adjusts later signalling. The same signal can have different effects when receptor distribution, concentration, timing, or developmental context differs.

A useful control-system diagram names the source, signal, route, target, response, and feedback. It should not draw every arrow as stimulation: some responses reduce upstream release, while the mid-cycle estrogen pattern can briefly support positive feedback.

sections.label: Scientific inquiry
sections.title: Questions must be investigable and respectful
paragraphs: A scientific question identifies variables that can be observed or measured and a population or model to which the evidence applies. Reproductive biology often involves private health information and ethically sensitive decisions. Classroom investigations should use anonymized, fictional, or synthetic evidence and avoid diagnosing a person or treating identity as a laboratory variable.

A strong question might ask how a hormone concentration changes across a modelled cycle or how temperature affects sperm production in a non-human model. It would not ask classmates to reveal experiences or use a small classroom sample to claim what all people should do.

conceptMap.title: Reproduction as an evidence system
conceptMap.description: Cell processes, organs, hormonal control, and development form a connected pathway with feedback and multiple evidence points.

nodes.label: Produce
nodes.detail: Meiosis and supporting tissues form gametes.

nodes.label: Coordinate
nodes.detail: Hormone signals align development, transport, and timing.

nodes.label: Develop
nodes.detail: Fertilization begins a regulated sequence of cell division and differentiation.

interaction.title: Reproductive-system connection board
interaction.intro: Compare three disruptions at different biological scales.
interaction.prompt: Choose a case, locate the disrupted step, and predict one downstream effect without overclaiming.

cases.label: Chromosome segregation
cases.evidence: A model gamete contains an unexpected chromosome number after meiosis.
cases.explanation: The evidence points to a segregation error during gamete formation; later outcomes depend on the chromosome involved and whether fertilization occurs.

cases.label: Hormone receptor block
cases.evidence: A target tissue does not respond even though the signalling hormone is present in blood.
cases.explanation: The signal is available, but receptor binding or downstream response is disrupted, so increasing the source is not automatically an effective correction.

cases.label: Transport obstruction
cases.evidence: Gametes are produced, but a reproductive duct is blocked.
cases.explanation: Production and transport are separate functions; a structural obstruction can reduce the chance that gametes meet without showing that gamete formation failed.

interaction.staticFallback: For every case, identify the scale, normal function, observed evidence, predicted consequence, and one fact still needed.

B.learningIntention: I am learning to connect male reproductive structures to sperm production, maturation, transport, and delivery.
successCriteria: I can identify the required male reproductive structures and state their functions.
I can distinguish sperm cells from the tissues and fluids that support them.
I can trace a sperm cell from a seminiferous tubule to the urethra and explain each transition.
B.materials: The local labelled anatomy model, pathway cards, and paper or the Investigation Notebook.
B.safety: Use anatomical terms accurately and respectfully. The lesson is educational and cannot assess an individual’s fertility, anatomy, hormone status, or health.

warmup.title: Production is not delivery
warmup.prompt: Why might normal sperm production and successful sperm delivery require different structures?
warmup.placeholder: Name one production function and one transport or support function.

sections.label: Production
sections.title: The testes contain specialized compartments
paragraphs: Seminiferous tubules are tightly coiled sites of spermatogenesis. Developing germ cells progress toward the tubule lumen while Sertoli cells provide structural support, nutrients, signalling, and a regulated local environment. Interstitial cells between tubules produce testosterone in response to LH. The scrotum helps maintain a temperature environment that supports sperm development.

A cross-section must distinguish the sperm lineage from supporting cells. Finding testosterone in blood does not show that mature sperm are present, and finding germ cells does not show that transport pathways are open.

sections.label: Maturation and transport
sections.title: Sperm change as they move through ducts
paragraphs: Sperm leaving seminiferous tubules are not yet fully motile. They pass into the epididymis, where they mature and are stored, then travel through a vas or ductus deferens during ejaculation. The ejaculatory duct joins glandular secretions with sperm before the mixture enters the urethra. Each structure has a distinct production, maturation, storage, or transport role.

Pathway evidence is read in order: testes and tubules, epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, and urethra. A blockage at one location predicts material upstream and reduced passage downstream.

sections.label: Accessory glands
sections.title: Semen contains more than sperm
paragraphs: Seminal vesicles, the prostate gland, and bulbourethral or Cowper’s glands contribute fluid to semen. Their secretions support transport and the chemical environment, but they do not manufacture sperm. The penis provides a route for semen delivery, while the urethra also carries urine at different times; regulatory mechanisms prevent simultaneous flow under typical conditions.
A sample can contain glandular fluid even when sperm count is low or zero. Therefore semen volume alone cannot establish sperm production, motility, morphology, or fertility.

sections.label: Function from structure
sections.title: Anatomical evidence supports bounded predictions
paragraphs: Structure-function reasoning asks what a tissue does, what moves through it, and what signal regulates it. It avoids treating an anatomy diagram as a list to memorize. A damaged Sertoli-cell environment, reduced LH signalling, an epididymal disruption, and a blocked ductus deferens would be expected to alter different steps and produce different evidence patterns.
To localize a disruption, compare hormone evidence, germ-cell development, semen composition, and pathway patency. One measurement rarely distinguishes every cause.

conceptMap.title: Sperm production-to-delivery pathway
conceptMap.description: Sperm develop in seminiferous tubules, mature in the epididymis, travel through ducts, combine with glandular fluids, and leave through the urethra.

nodes.label: Produce
nodes.detail: Seminiferous tubules and Sertoli cells support spermatogenesis; interstitial cells produce testosterone.

nodes.label: Mature and move
nodes.detail: The epididymis and ductus deferens mature, store, and transport sperm.

nodes.label: Support and deliver
nodes.detail: Accessory glands add fluid before semen moves through the urethra.

interaction.title: Male anatomy pathway tracer
interaction.intro: Use location and evidence to distinguish production, maturation, support, and transport.
interaction.prompt: Choose a case and identify the most directly affected structure-function link.

cases.label: Tubule support disrupted
cases.evidence: LH and testosterone are within the model range, but developing germ cells show poor survival inside seminiferous tubules.
cases.explanation: The pattern points toward impaired Sertoli-cell support or the tubule environment rather than a simple absence of interstitial-cell testosterone production.

cases.label: Maturation disrupted
cases.evidence: Sperm cells leave the testes but show reduced maturation and motility before ejaculation.
cases.explanation: The epididymis is the strongest anatomical location because sperm mature and are stored there after production.

cases.label: Transport obstructed
cases.evidence: Sperm production markers are present, but sperm are absent downstream of one duct.
cases.explanation: A ductus deferens obstruction separates successful production from unsuccessful transport and predicts accumulation upstream.

interaction.staticFallback: Trace the normal route and mark where the first mismatch between upstream and downstream evidence appears.

B.learningIntention: I am learning to connect female reproductive structures, follicle development, oogenesis, fertilization, and implantation.
successCriteria: I can identify the required female reproductive structures and state their functions.
I can distinguish an oocyte from its follicle and a corpus luteum.
I can trace an oocyte or early embryo through the reproductive tract and predict effects of a localized disruption.
B.materials: The local anatomy and follicle-development models and the supplied pathway evidence.
B.safety: Use anatomical and developmental terms respectfully. This model does not determine an individual’s fertility, cycle, pregnancy status, anatomy, or health.

warmup.title: Cell and support system
warmup.prompt: What is the difference between an oocyte and the follicle that surrounds it?
warmup.placeholder: Describe the cell and at least one support function.

sections.label: Ovarian structure
sections.title: Follicles support a developing oocyte
paragraphs: The ovaries contain follicles at different stages. A follicle includes an oocyte plus surrounding cells that support development and participate in hormone production. Usually one dominant follicle reaches ovulation in a cycle. After ovulation, the remaining follicular tissue becomes the corpus luteum, a temporary endocrine structure that produces progesterone and estrogen.
An image of a follicle is not an image of an egg alone. Evidence about follicle size, ovulation, and corpus-luteum activity must be interpreted as a changing tissue sequence.

sections.label: Anatomical pathway
sections.title: The uterine tube connects ovulation to the uterus
paragraphs: After ovulation, fimbriae and fluid movement help guide the secondary oocyte into a uterine or Fallopian tube. Fertilization typically occurs in the tube, not the uterus. Cilia and smooth-muscle contractions help move the early embryo toward the uterus. The cervix forms the lower opening of the uterus, and the vagina connects the cervix to the exterior.
A pathway model should not draw the ovary directly connected to the tube. The oocyte crosses a small body-cavity space, and successful fertilization does not guarantee transport or implantation.

sections.label: Uterine environment
sections.title: The endometrium changes across the cycle
paragraphs: The uterus has a muscular wall and an inner endometrium that responds to ovarian hormones. Estrogen supports proliferative growth, while progesterone supports a secretory environment after ovulation. If implantation does not occur and ovarian hormone support declines, much of the functional endometrial layer is shed during menstruation.
Endometrial thickness is one evidence stream, not a complete fertility measure. Timing, hormone patterns, embryo development, anatomy, and many other factors affect reproductive outcomes.

sections.label: Oogenesis
sections.title: Oocyte meiosis includes pauses
paragraphs: Oogenesis begins before birth. Primary oocytes pause in prophase I, and selected oocytes resume meiosis after puberty. A secondary oocyte is ovulated after completing meiosis I and pauses again in metaphase II. Completion of meiosis II normally follows fertilization. Unequal cytoplasmic division produces one large ovum and small polar bodies rather than four similar gametes.
Chromosome state and cell name depend on the stage. Calling every ovarian germ cell an ovum hides the meiotic pauses and the distinction between a primary oocyte, secondary oocyte, and mature ovum.

conceptMap.title: Oocyte-to-implantation pathway
conceptMap.description: A follicle supports oocyte development, ovulation releases a secondary oocyte, the uterine tube is the usual fertilization site, and the uterus provides the implantation environment.

nodes.label: Develop
nodes.detail: An ovarian follicle supports a maturing oocyte.

nodes.label: Move and fertilize
nodes.detail: The secondary oocyte enters a uterine tube, where fertilization may occur.

nodes.label: Prepare and implant
nodes.detail: The early embryo reaches a hormone-responsive endometrium.

interaction.title: Female anatomy evidence locator
interaction.intro: Use the first location where evidence changes to distinguish ovarian, tubal, and uterine mechanisms.
interaction.prompt: Choose a case and identify the most direct structure-function explanation.

cases.label: Follicle maturation
cases.evidence: A model shows low follicle growth and no dominant follicle before the expected ovulation window.
cases.explanation: The strongest first question concerns ovarian follicle development and its hormonal support, before making claims about transport or implantation.

cases.label: Tubal transport
cases.evidence: Ovulation and fertilization markers are present, but movement toward the uterus is obstructed in one tube.
cases.explanation: The uterine tube has a transport role after ovulation and fertilization; an obstruction separates these events from successful arrival in the uterus.

cases.label: Endometrial response
cases.evidence: Ovulation is supported by evidence, but the endometrium shows little secretory response during the luteal phase.
cases.explanation: The pattern directs attention to progesterone signalling or endometrial responsiveness rather than assuming ovulation itself failed.

interaction.staticFallback: Place each event—follicle development, ovulation, fertilization, transport, endometrial preparation, implantation—at its anatomical location before interpreting the case.

B.learningIntention: I am learning to explain how chromosomes, genes, hormones, receptors, and timing influence reproductive development without erasing biological variation.
successCriteria: I can distinguish chromosomal, gonadal, hormonal, anatomical, and secondary-sex-characteristic evidence.
I can explain a simplified SRY-and-androgen pathway and state its limits.
I can interpret a developmental case without making assumptions about identity or treating variation as a value judgment.
B.materials: The local developmental-pathway model and three fictional evidence cases.
B.safety: Sex traits and gender are related concepts but are not interchangeable. Use respectful language, do not label variation as more or less human, and never infer a learner’s biology or identity.

warmup.title: One label cannot describe every level
warmup.prompt: Why can a chromosome result alone be insufficient to predict all reproductive structures or a person’s identity?
warmup.placeholder: Name at least two later steps or sources of variation.

sections.label: Developmental sequence
sections.title: Chromosomes influence—but do not single-handedly determine—development
paragraphs: At fertilization, chromosomes establish one part of a developmental context. In a common simplified pathway, an SRY gene on a Y chromosome initiates testis development. Gonadal tissue then produces signals, including androgens and anti-Müllerian hormone, that influence reproductive-tract and external-anatomy development. Each step depends on gene expression, timing, hormone synthesis, transport, receptors, and tissue response.

A pathway diagram is a model of common mechanisms, not a complete classification system. Variations in chromosomes, gene location or expression, gonadal development, hormone synthesis, receptors, and target tissues can produce diverse combinations of sex traits.

sections.label: Signal and response
sections.title: A hormone effect requires a responsive target
paragraphs: Testosterone can support development of Wolffian-duct derivatives, while conversion to dihydrotestosterone contributes to development of some external structures. A hormone concentration alone does not establish an effect. The hormone must reach cells with functional receptors and downstream signalling. Different tissues can respond differently at different developmental times.

When androgen is present but a predicted response is absent, examine receptor or target-tissue evidence before concluding that the hormone was not produced. This is the same source-signal-target logic used elsewhere in endocrine biology.

sections.label: Multiple dimensions
sections.title: Sex traits and gender require precise language
paragraphs: Chromosomes, genes, gonads, internal and external anatomy, hormone patterns, secondary sex characteristics, fertility, and gender identity are distinct dimensions. They may correlate in common patterns but are not synonyms. Gender also includes social and personal dimensions that cannot be read from a karyotype, anatomy image, or hormone value.

Scientific communication should name the measured trait rather than substituting a broad label. For example, report an XY karyotype, a receptor result, or a hormone concentration—not an unsupported conclusion about identity, behaviour, or worth.

sections.label: Model limits
sections.title: Development is probabilistic and context-dependent
paragraphs: A developmental pathway supports predictions about mechanisms, but it does not make every body identical or predict every life outcome. Genetic variants, mosaicism, environmental context, medical intervention, and ordinary variation can alter traits. Clinical interpretation requires qualified professionals, consent, and more evidence than a classroom case provides.
In a fictional case, state which pathway step is supported, which alternative remains plausible, and what evidence would distinguish them. Do not diagnose or recommend treatment.

conceptMap.title: Chromosome-to-tissue response pathway
conceptMap.description: Chromosomal and gene evidence can influence gonadal development, hormone production, receptor-mediated tissue response, and reproductive anatomy, with variation possible at every step.

nodes.label: Initiate
nodes.detail: Genes such as SRY can influence gonadal development in a common pathway.

nodes.label: Signal
nodes.detail: Developing gonads can release hormones that circulate to targets.

nodes.label: Respond
nodes.detail: Receptors, timing, and tissue context shape anatomical outcomes.

interaction.title: Sex-development evidence pathway
interaction.intro: Compare three fictional cases in which chromosome, hormone, and tissue-response evidence do not all align in the same way.
interaction.prompt: Locate the earliest supported divergence and identify what the evidence cannot establish.

cases.label: Gene-location variation
cases.evidence: A fictional karyotype lacks a visible Y chromosome, but an SRY-region test is positive and testicular tissue developed.
cases.explanation: Gene location and expression provide more direct pathway evidence than chromosome appearance alone; the case does not determine identity or every anatomical trait.

cases.label: Target-response variation
cases.evidence: Testosterone is present, but cultured target cells show little androgen-receptor response.
cases.explanation: The pattern supports a target-response difference rather than absent hormone production and illustrates why source, signal, receptor, and response must be separated.

cases.label: Hormone-conversion variation
cases.evidence: Testosterone is present, while a model shows reduced conversion to dihydrotestosterone in selected tissues.
cases.explanation: A conversion step can change some androgen-dependent outcomes without implying that all sex traits, fertility, or identity follow one pattern.

interaction.staticFallback: For each fictional case, create columns for chromosome/gene evidence, gonadal evidence, hormone evidence, receptor response, anatomy, and conclusions that remain unsupported.

warmup.title: Signal or response?
warmup.prompt: A hormone concentration rises, but its target response does not. What two explanations should be considered before assuming the source failed?
warmup.placeholder: Consider transport, receptors, and downstream response.

sections.label: Axis
sections.title: GnRH starts a multi-level signalling pathway
paragraphs: Neurons in the hypothalamus release gonadotropin-releasing hormone into vessels that reach the anterior pituitary. GnRH stimulates pituitary gonadotroph cells to release FSH and LH. These gonadotropins travel through blood to gonadal targets. Their effects differ because ovarian and testicular cells express different receptors and carry out different responses.
A diagram should identify each hormone source and target. GnRH is not released by the gonads, and FSH and LH do not simply become estrogen, progesterone, or testosterone.

sections.label: Ovarian targets
sections.title: FSH and LH coordinate changing ovarian tissues
paragraphs: FSH supports follicle growth and estrogen production. LH acts on ovarian cells and, during the mid-cycle surge, supports ovulation and corpus-luteum formation. The corpus luteum releases progesterone and estrogen. These ovarian hormones affect reproductive tissues and return feedback to the hypothalamus and pituitary.

The same estrogen signal can participate in negative feedback through much of the cycle and in a temporary positive-feedback pattern near ovulation. Direction depends on concentration, timing, and system state.

sections.label: Testicular targets
sections.title: FSH and LH support sperm production through different cells
paragraphs: LH stimulates interstitial cells to produce testosterone. FSH acts mainly through Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis. Testosterone contributes to reproductive-organ function and secondary sex characteristics and usually provides negative feedback to hypothalamic and pituitary signalling. Sperm production therefore depends on both local support and endocrine coordination.
Low sperm production cannot be explained from testosterone alone. FSH signalling, Sertoli-cell function, temperature, germ-cell integrity, transport, and other factors also matter.

sections.label: Feedback reasoning
sections.title: Use upstream and downstream values together
paragraphs: Negative feedback stabilizes a regulated pathway: a downstream hormone or response reduces upstream stimulation. If a gonadal hormone is low and pituitary gonadotropins are high, the pituitary appears to be responding to weak downstream feedback. If both are low, an upstream signalling difference becomes more plausible. These are model-based patterns, not diagnoses.
Interpret at least two levels and compare the observed direction with the feedback prediction. A single high or low value without timing, reference context, and repeated evidence is insufficient.

warmup.title: Read before explaining
warmup.prompt: What three graph features should you describe before naming the biological event that may explain them?
warmup.placeholder: Consider direction, timing, magnitude, units, and comparison.

sections.label: Cycle alignment
sections.title: Ovarian and uterine cycles are coordinated but distinct
paragraphs: The ovarian cycle includes follicular development, ovulation, and the luteal phase. The uterine cycle includes menstrual, proliferative, and secretory patterns in the endometrium. Hormone signals link the two, but the labels describe events in different organs. Day 1 is conventionally the first day of menstrual bleeding in a cycle record.
Align every observation on one time axis before explaining. A uterine event should not be mislabeled as an ovarian structure, and a hormone peak should not be treated as the event itself.

sections.label: Follicular phase
sections.title: Follicle growth changes estrogen and feedback
paragraphs: Early in the model cycle, reduced ovarian-hormone feedback permits FSH support of follicle development. Growing follicles produce increasing estrogen. Estrogen supports endometrial proliferation and usually contributes negative feedback. When estrogen remains high in an appropriate context, feedback can shift and support a rapid LH surge.
The mid-cycle LH surge is a strong temporal clue for imminent ovulation in the simplified model, but a classroom graph does not confirm ovulation in a real person.

sections.label: Luteal phase
sections.title: The corpus luteum supports a secretory endometrium
paragraphs: After ovulation, LH-supported follicular tissue becomes the corpus luteum. Progesterone rises, with estrogen, and supports a thicker, secretory endometrium. These hormones also provide negative feedback that generally reduces FSH and LH. If implantation does not occur, corpus-luteum function declines and ovarian hormone concentrations fall.

The decline in progesterone and estrogen helps explain endometrial shedding and the start of a new cycle record. The graph relationship is temporal and mechanistic, not a claim that every cycle has identical values or timing.

sections.label: Investigation
sections.title: Graph interpretation needs variables and uncertainty
paragraphs: A cycle-data investigation defines time as the independent variable and hormone concentration or tissue measure as a dependent variable. A good graph includes units, a readable scale, distinct traces, and annotations that separate observed peaks from inferred events. Replication and variation should be shown when available.

A conclusion should cite specific days or relative changes, connect them to a feedback mechanism, and state that synthetic values simplify pulsatile release, individual variation, measurement uncertainty, and cycle diversity.

warmup.title: Infection and symptoms are not the same
warmup.prompt: Why can absence of symptoms be weak evidence that a sexually transmitted infection is absent?
warmup.placeholder: Connect asymptomatic infection to testing and transmission.

sections.label: Mechanism
sections.title: STIs can affect reproduction through different pathways
paragraphs: Sexually transmitted infections are caused by different pathogens and do not have one shared effect. Chlamydia and gonorrhea can infect reproductive-tract tissues and, when untreated, may contribute to inflammation, scarring, pelvic inflammatory disease, or epididymal complications that can affect fertility. HPV infects epithelial cells; persistent high-risk types can contribute to precancerous changes and cancers.

Risk depends on pathogen, site, duration, immune response, access to care, and treatment. Infection does not make a person irresponsible, and a positive test does not establish when or from whom transmission occurred.

sections.label: Prevention layers
sections.title: No single prevention tool does every job
paragraphs: Barrier methods can reduce transmission risk for many infections but protection depends on correct and consistent use and on whether infected skin lies outside the covered area. Vaccination can prevent infection from selected HPV types but does not treat an existing infection or prevent every STI. Regular testing can identify some asymptomatic infections, while treatment options depend on the pathogen.
A defensible prevention plan matches the tool to the transmission route and evidence. It avoids absolute claims such as “always safe” or “zero risk” and uses current public-health guidance.

sections.label: Fertility evidence
sections.title: Fertility is a multi-factor probability
paragraphs: Fertility can be influenced by gamete production and quality, anatomy and transport, hormone coordination, timing, age-related changes, infections, environmental exposures, and chance. Infertility is not established by one classroom variable. Evaluation may involve both partners or gamete sources because reproductive outcomes arise from interacting factors.

When a case includes a prior infection and a transport obstruction, the mechanism can be discussed as plausible evidence without saying the infection is the only cause or that conception is impossible.

sections.label: Health communication
sections.title: Evidence-based decisions require consent and access
paragraphs: Health decisions involve scientific evidence, values, privacy, consent, cost, access, culture, and relationships. Respectful communication uses person-centred, non-stigmatizing language and avoids assumptions about partners, anatomy, orientation, gender, pregnancy intentions, or behaviour. Public-health recommendations should be distinguished from moral judgments.

A high-quality evidence brief identifies the question, uses an authoritative current source, explains benefit and limitation, and directs individual medical decisions to qualified care rather than a classroom conclusion.

conceptMap.title: Layered reproductive-health protection
conceptMap.description: Transmission prevention, vaccination where available, testing, pathogen-appropriate treatment, and respectful communication address different parts of reproductive health.

nodes.label: Reduce exposure
nodes.detail: Barrier practices and informed choices can reduce—but not eliminate—risk.

nodes.label: Prevent and detect
nodes.detail: Vaccination prevents selected infections; testing can identify infections without symptoms.

nodes.label: Treat and follow up
nodes.detail: Qualified care matches treatment and follow-up to pathogen and person.

B.safety: Use biological terms without assigning blame for pregnancy outcomes. This simplified model cannot determine pregnancy status, viability, fertility, or an individual’s medical care.

warmup.title: Two locations, two events
warmup.prompt: Where does fertilization usually occur, where does implantation occur, and why must the developing structure move between them?
warmup.placeholder: Name both anatomical locations and the transport step.

sections.label: Gamete meeting
sections.title: Fertilization usually begins in a uterine tube
paragraphs: Sperm that reach the female reproductive tract undergo functional changes collectively described as capacitation. One sperm may bind and cross cell layers around the secondary oocyte, undergo an acrosome reaction, and fuse with the oocyte membrane. Membrane and cortical changes reduce additional sperm fusion. Fertilization is a sequence, not an instantaneous collision.
Evidence of sperm presence does not establish membrane fusion, and membrane fusion does not by itself establish normal chromosome segregation or development.

sections.label: Chromosome union
sections.title: Meiosis finishes before parental chromosomes combine
paragraphs: Sperm entry typically triggers completion of meiosis II in the secondary oocyte. Male and female pronuclei form, DNA is prepared, and parental chromosome sets contribute to the first mitotic division. The resulting zygote is diploid, but its chromosomes remain organized through a changing cell-cycle sequence.
Use cell stage and chromosome state precisely. A secondary oocyte before completion of meiosis II is not identical to the post-fertilization zygote.

sections.label: Cleavage
sections.title: Cell number rises before overall size rises
paragraphs: The zygote undergoes cleavage divisions as it travels toward the uterus. Cells called blastomeres become smaller because the overall conceptus remains within the zona pellucida during early divisions. A morula stage precedes a blastocyst with an outer trophoblast, an inner cell mass, and a fluid-filled cavity.
A larger cell count during cleavage does not mean the conceptus has grown proportionally. Stage interpretation uses organization, location, and timing together.

sections.label: Implantation
sections.title: A blastocyst must interact with a receptive endometrium
paragraphs: After hatching from the zona pellucida, the blastocyst can attach to and begin embedding in the endometrium. Trophoblast-derived tissues contribute to early support and release hCG, which helps maintain the corpus luteum and progesterone production. Implantation depends on embryo development, transport, timing, and endometrial receptivity.
A positive hCG-related signal is evidence of trophoblast activity, not a complete forecast of development. Fertilization, implantation, and ongoing pregnancy are distinct evidence thresholds.

conceptMap.title: Fertilization-to-implantation sequence
conceptMap.description: Gamete membrane fusion and completion of meiosis produce a zygote, cleavage forms a morula and blastocyst during transport, and trophoblast tissue begins implantation in the endometrium.

nodes.label: Fertilize
nodes.detail: Gamete recognition and fusion support a diploid zygote.

nodes.label: Divide and travel
nodes.detail: Cleavage produces smaller blastomeres, a morula, and a blastocyst.

nodes.label: Implant
nodes.detail: A hatched blastocyst interacts with a receptive endometrium.

interaction.title: Early-development sequence lab
interaction.intro: Use location, organization, and hormone evidence to identify an early developmental stage.
interaction.prompt: Choose a case and place it in the sequence with one justified uncertainty.

cases.label: Cleavage in transit
cases.evidence: Several small blastomeres remain inside a zona pellucida while the structure is in a uterine tube.
cases.explanation: The evidence fits early cleavage during transport; increased cell number has not yet produced a proportional increase in overall size.

cases.label: Blastocyst organization
cases.evidence: A fluid cavity, outer cell layer, and inner cell cluster are visible near the uterine cavity.

cases.label: Trophoblast signal

B.learningIntention: I am learning to explain how extra-embryonic membranes and the placenta support exchange, protection, and development.
successCriteria: I can distinguish amnion, chorion, allantois, umbilical vessels, and placenta by function.
I can explain maternal-fetal exchange without saying the two blood supplies normally mix directly.
I can interpret a transfer case by considering molecular properties, gradients, transport, and placental limits.

warmup.title: Close exchange without direct mixing
warmup.prompt: How could oxygen move from maternal blood to fetal blood if the two blood supplies normally remain in separate vessels?
warmup.placeholder: Describe a barrier, gradient, and exchange surface.

sections.label: Membranes
sections.title: Temporary structures carry distinct support roles
paragraphs: The amnion encloses the fluid-filled amniotic cavity, cushioning the developing embryo or fetus and permitting movement. The chorion contributes to the fetal portion of the placenta and forms villous exchange surfaces. The allantois contributes to structures associated with the umbilical cord and urinary bladder development. These are extra-embryonic tissues even though they arise from the conceptus.
A membrane should be identified by location and function, not by calling every surrounding layer the placenta. The terms describe related but non-identical structures.

sections.label: Placental exchange
sections.title: Maternal and fetal circulation approach across a barrier
paragraphs: Maternal blood enters spaces around chorionic villi, while fetal blood travels through vessels within the villi. Thin exchange surfaces and extensive area support movement of gases, nutrients, wastes, water, ions, and selected molecules. Oxygen typically moves toward fetal blood, while carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes move toward maternal circulation.

The maternal and fetal blood supplies normally remain separated by tissue layers. Describing the placenta as a filter is too simple because transfer depends on molecular size, lipid solubility, charge, transport proteins, concentration gradients, metabolism, and gestational stage.

sections.label: Endocrine support
sections.title: The placenta also becomes an endocrine organ
paragraphs: Early hCG supports the corpus luteum, helping maintain progesterone production. As pregnancy progresses, placental tissues produce increasing amounts of progesterone and estrogen that support uterine conditions and contribute to physiological changes. Placental signals interact with maternal systems rather than replacing every endocrine pathway.
Hormone timing matters. The same hCG concentration has different meaning depending on developmental stage, trend, assay, and clinical context; classroom values cannot determine viability.

sections.label: Limits and protection
sections.title: A barrier reduces some risks but is not absolute
paragraphs: The placenta contributes immune, metabolic, transport, and endocrine functions, yet some pathogens, medications, drugs, alcohol, and environmental chemicals can reach or affect developing tissues. Transfer does not guarantee harm, and absence of transfer does not guarantee safety, because dose, timing, genetics, metabolism, and tissue sensitivity matter.
An exposure claim needs a named substance, route, dose, timing, evidence quality, and outcome. Individual decisions belong with qualified care and current authoritative guidance.

conceptMap.title: Maternal-fetal exchange interface
conceptMap.description: Maternal blood surrounds chorionic villi, fetal blood remains in villous vessels, substances cross placental tissues selectively, and the placenta also produces hormones.

nodes.label: Maternal side

nodes.label: Exchange surface
nodes.detail: Placental tissues mediate selective transfer and metabolism.

nodes.label: Fetal side
nodes.detail: Umbilical vessels carry fetal blood to and from the exchange surface.

cases.label: Oxygen gradient
cases.evidence: Maternal blood arriving near villi has a higher oxygen partial pressure than fetal blood arriving through umbilical arteries.
cases.explanation: The gradient and exchange surface support net oxygen movement toward fetal blood without direct blood mixing.

cases.label: Glucose transport
cases.evidence: Fetal glucose availability tracks maternal concentration but requires placental transport proteins.

cases.label: Large-molecule limit

cases.explanation: Molecular size, charge, receptor-mediated routes, and placental biology constrain transfer, so one small-molecule rule cannot be applied to every substance.

B.learningIntention: I am learning to connect gastrulation, germ layers, differentiation, and organogenesis in a developmental evidence map.
successCriteria: I can explain why gastrulation changes cell position and developmental potential.
I can identify major ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm derivatives required by the curriculum.
I can use location, gene expression, and tissue evidence without saying one germ layer acts alone.
B.materials: The local germ-layer fate map, colour-independent labels, and supplied differentiation evidence.
B.safety: This is a simplified developmental model. It cannot predict an individual pregnancy outcome or attribute an observed condition to one event without clinical evidence.

warmup.title: Same genome, different cell
warmup.prompt: If most cells contain the same DNA, what can make a neuron and a muscle cell develop different structures and functions?
warmup.placeholder: Connect gene regulation, signals, position, and differentiation.

sections.label: Gastrulation
sections.title: Cell movement establishes body organization
paragraphs: Gastrulation transforms an early embryo into a structure with three primary germ layers and body axes. Cells move, change neighbours, and receive new signals. The event is not simply “three coloured sheets appearing”; position and interaction influence which genes are expressed and which developmental pathways remain available.

A fate map is probabilistic and stage-specific. It supports where tissues commonly arise but does not mean a mature organ descends from only one cell layer or forms without induction from neighbouring tissues.

sections.label: Ectoderm
sections.title: Ectoderm contributes to interfaces and nervous tissue
paragraphs: Ectoderm contributes to the epidermis and nervous system, including specialized structures that arise through folding and induction. Neural ectoderm forms the neural tube, while neural crest cells migrate widely and contribute to several tissue types. Surface ectoderm contributes to epidermal and selected sensory structures.
Calling ectoderm only “skin and brain” misses developmental transitions and neural-crest contributions. Trace a tissue through intermediate structures when explaining evidence.

sections.label: Mesoderm
sections.title: Mesoderm supports movement, transport, and internal structure
paragraphs: Mesoderm contributes to skeletal and muscular tissues, connective tissues, blood and much of the cardiovascular system, kidneys, gonads, and many reproductive structures. Regional mesoderm receives different signals, so its derivatives are not one uniform tissue family.
An organ such as the digestive tract includes mesoderm-derived muscle and connective tissue around an endoderm-derived epithelial lining. Mixed developmental origin is common.

sections.label: Endoderm and organogenesis
sections.title: Endoderm contributes to internal linings and glands
paragraphs: Endoderm contributes to much of the epithelial lining of digestive and respiratory systems and to tissues in organs such as the liver, pancreas, thyroid, and other endocrine structures. Organogenesis depends on reciprocal signals among germ layers, controlled cell division, migration, programmed cell death, and differentiation.
A tissue’s germ-layer origin does not by itself explain final organ shape or function. Use gene-expression, position, and interaction evidence to connect early layer to mature structure.

conceptMap.title: Gastrulation-to-organogenesis pathway
conceptMap.description: Cell movements establish germ layers, local signals guide differentiation, tissues interact, and organs acquire complex structures from multiple developmental origins.

nodes.label: Reposition
nodes.detail: Gastrulation establishes layers and body axes.

nodes.label: Differentiate
nodes.detail: Signals and gene regulation change cell identity and potential.

nodes.label: Integrate
nodes.detail: Multiple tissues interact during morphogenesis and organogenesis.

interaction.title: Germ-layer fate mapper
interaction.intro: Use tissue evidence to select the strongest primary germ-layer origin while recognizing mixed-organ origins.
interaction.prompt: Choose a case, justify the primary origin, and name a contributing tissue from another layer where relevant.

cases.label: Neural tissue
cases.evidence: A developing structure folds from dorsal outer tissue and later forms neurons of the central nervous system.
cases.explanation: The evidence supports ectoderm through neural ectoderm and neural-tube development.

cases.label: Skeletal muscle

cases.explanation: The evidence supports mesodermal origin and illustrates regional differentiation within mesoderm.

cases.label: Digestive epithelium

cases.explanation: The epithelial lining is primarily endoderm-derived, while surrounding muscle and connective tissues include mesodermal contributions.

B.learningIntention: I am learning to explain major prenatal developmental patterns and evaluate environmental-exposure evidence by dose, timing, route, and uncertainty.
successCriteria: I can distinguish embryonic and fetal periods and summarize major trimester patterns without treating them as exact deadlines.
I can explain why exposure timing and dose can change developmental effects.
I can interpret an exposure dataset without assigning blame, diagnosing an outcome, or claiming that association proves causation.
B.materials: The local prenatal-development timeline and a clearly labelled synthetic exposure dataset.
B.safety: Exposure and pregnancy questions can be sensitive. Use fictional data, avoid blame, and direct personal questions about alcohol, medications, drugs, infection, radiation, or pregnancy to qualified prenatal care or poison-control/public-health services as appropriate.

warmup.title: Timing changes vulnerability
warmup.prompt: Why might the same exposure have different effects before implantation, during organ formation, and during later fetal growth?
warmup.placeholder: Connect developmental process, dose, and timing.

sections.label: Developmental periods
sections.title: Embryonic and fetal development emphasize different processes
paragraphs: The embryonic period includes implantation, gastrulation, body-plan establishment, and early organogenesis. The fetal period emphasizes growth, maturation, and increasing functional integration, although development continues across the entire pregnancy. Trimester labels are useful broad time windows, not sharp biological switches that occur at identical moments in every pregnancy.
A developmental timeline should show overlapping processes and uncertainty. “Formed” does not mean fully mature or independent, and later growth can remain sensitive to environmental conditions.

sections.label: Exposure framework
sections.title: Risk depends on substance, dose, route, timing, and response
paragraphs: A teratogen is an environmental agent that can disrupt development under particular exposure conditions. Potential effects depend on dose and duration, route, placental transfer, developmental timing, genetics, metabolism, nutrition, co-exposures, and access to care. Alcohol, selected drugs, certain infections, and ionizing radiation have different mechanisms and evidence bases.
The statement “all exposures are equally harmful” is inaccurate, as is “a small exposure is always safe.” Individual guidance must come from current authoritative clinical sources.

sections.label: Evidence quality
sections.title: Human developmental evidence has ethical and methodological limits
paragraphs: Randomized exposure studies are usually unethical, so evidence often comes from observational studies, registries, case patterns, animal models, cellular models, and mechanistic knowledge. Confounding can occur when an exposure is correlated with nutrition, stress, health conditions, other substances, or access to care. Multiple converging evidence types strengthen causal inference.

A group-level association does not predict an individual outcome with certainty. Report absolute context, sample, comparison, uncertainty, and plausible mechanism rather than a headline-only relative risk.

sections.label: Communication
sections.title: Prevention messages should inform without blame
paragraphs: Public-health communication aims to reduce preventable harm while recognizing addiction, unequal access, incomplete information, coercion, stigma, and social determinants. Accurate guidance can be direct without treating pregnancy outcomes as evidence of moral character. When exposure has occurred, seeking timely care is more useful than withholding information because of shame.

An evidence brief should separate established guidance from uncertainty, name available supports, and avoid language that isolates responsibility from partners, systems, workplaces, or healthcare access.

B.learningIntention: I am learning to explain how hormonal, mechanical, and neural feedback coordinate parturition and lactation.
successCriteria: I can trace a positive-feedback loop involving cervical stretch, oxytocin, and uterine contraction.
I can distinguish milk production from milk ejection and identify prolactin and oxytocin roles.
I can explain why a simplified feedback model does not predict labour timing or feeding outcomes for an individual.

warmup.title: When feedback amplifies
warmup.prompt: How is positive feedback useful in a process that must move rapidly toward a clear endpoint?
warmup.placeholder: Name the stimulus, amplified response, and endpoint.

sections.label: Parturition
sections.title: Labour emerges from interacting signals
paragraphs: Near parturition, changes in uterine, placental, fetal, and cervical signalling increase uterine readiness and contractility. Prostaglandins contribute to cervical and uterine changes, and oxytocin supports contractions. No single hormone acts as an isolated on-switch in every labour; receptor abundance, tissue readiness, fetal signals, and mechanical stretch interact.
A model that shows only “oxytocin causes birth” omits the changing tissue context and feedback that make the same signal more effective near labour.

sections.label: Positive feedback
sections.title: Cervical stretch can amplify contractions
paragraphs: As contractions move the fetus and increase cervical stretch, sensory information reaches the brain, promoting additional oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary. Oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions, which can increase stretch further. The loop amplifies until delivery changes the stimulus and ends the cycle.
Positive feedback is not inherently harmful or unstable; it is useful when a process has a defined endpoint. The loop differs from negative feedback, which counters a deviation.

sections.label: Milk production
sections.title: Prolactin supports synthesis
paragraphs: After delivery, changing placental-hormone conditions allow prolactin to support milk production in mammary gland tissue. Suckling-related neural signals can promote prolactin release and help sustain supply. Production depends on endocrine, neural, tissue, feeding, and health contexts and varies among individuals.
Prolactin is linked primarily to production in the simplified model. A single concentration does not establish milk volume, infant intake, comfort, or feeding success.

sections.label: Milk ejection
sections.title: Oxytocin supports a separate reflex
paragraphs: Suckling activates sensory pathways that promote oxytocin release. Oxytocin causes myoepithelial cells around milk-producing structures to contract, supporting milk ejection or let-down. Production and ejection are related but distinct; difficulty in one does not prove failure of the other.

A complete lactation model names sensory stimulus, neural pathway, pituitary signal, target cells, response, and feedback. It also recognizes that feeding method and support decisions involve health, access, culture, and individual needs.

B.learningIntention: I am learning to compare reproductive technologies by mechanism, evidence, risk, access, ethics, and the decision they are designed to support.
successCriteria: I can explain the physiological or mechanical basis of selected conception-control, assisted-reproduction, and infertility-reversal technologies.
I can compare effectiveness evidence using the correct outcome and time frame.
I can write a balanced technology brief that includes uncertainty, consent, access, and multiple perspectives.
B.materials: The local reproductive-technology comparison matrix and fictional decision cases.
B.safety: This lesson does not recommend a contraceptive, fertility treatment, surgery, or pregnancy decision. Individual choices require informed consent and qualified, current healthcare advice.

warmup.title: Match evidence to the decision
warmup.prompt: Why is a technology’s biological mechanism not enough to decide whether it is appropriate for a particular person?
warmup.placeholder: Add effectiveness, risk, values, access, reversibility, and goals.

sections.label: Conception control
sections.title: Technologies act at different reproductive steps
paragraphs: Conception-control methods may reduce the probability of ovulation, sperm transport, sperm survival, fertilization, or implantation-related conditions, depending on the method. Barrier methods act mechanically, hormonal methods change endocrine and reproductive-tissue conditions, intrauterine devices have local mechanisms, and sterilization interrupts gamete transport. No method should be described by a mechanism it does not use.
Compare typical-use and perfect-use evidence only when the source defines the outcome and time frame. Protection against pregnancy and protection against STI transmission are separate questions.

sections.label: Assisted reproduction
sections.title: IVF separates fertilization from the body before transfer
paragraphs: In vitro fertilization may involve controlled ovarian stimulation, oocyte retrieval, sperm preparation, fertilization or injection in a laboratory, embryo culture, and transfer to the uterus. Additional options can include donor gametes, cryopreservation, or testing in regulated contexts. Each step has its own success probabilities, risks, limits, and ethical considerations.

A success rate must name the denominator—cycle started, retrieval, transfer, clinical pregnancy, or live birth—and the population. One percentage cannot be moved across ages, clinics, or definitions without context.

sections.label: Reversal and repair
sections.title: Restoring a pathway does not guarantee conception
paragraphs: Some infertility interventions remove an obstruction, repair anatomy, reverse a prior sterilization procedure, support ovulation, or assist sperm delivery. Mechanical patency can be restored without correcting gamete quality, age-related probability, endocrine factors, uterine conditions, or other contributors. “Reversal” describes a procedure, not a guaranteed outcome.
Evaluate the step the technology changes and the later steps it cannot control. A pathway diagram prevents a local intervention from being confused with total reproductive success.

sections.label: STS decision
sections.title: Technology decisions combine evidence and values
paragraphs: Reproductive technologies can expand capability while raising questions about risk, embryo disposition, privacy, access, cost, equity, disability perspectives, cultural or religious values, donor relationships, legal rules, and long-term follow-up. Scientific evidence can clarify mechanisms and probabilities but cannot choose a person’s values.

A balanced brief represents perspectives accurately, uses current authoritative evidence, identifies who bears costs and risks, and distinguishes disagreement about values from disagreement about facts.

conceptMap.title: Reproductive-technology decision pathway
conceptMap.description: Identify the reproductive step, describe the technology’s mechanism, evaluate outcome evidence and risk, then integrate consent, access, values, and alternatives.

nodes.label: Decide in context

B.learningIntention: I am learning to integrate reproductive anatomy, hormonal control, development, environmental evidence, and technology in one unfamiliar case.
successCriteria: I can organize mixed evidence by biological scale, time, and pathway step.
I can compare at least two explanations and identify discriminating evidence.
I can recommend a next evidence step without diagnosing, prescribing, or treating uncertainty as failure.

warmup.title: Start with the evidence architecture
warmup.prompt: How will you keep an anatomy clue, a hormone graph, a developmental timeline, and a technology statistic from being mixed into one unsupported conclusion?
warmup.placeholder: Propose categories, sequence, and a method for comparing explanations.

sections.label: Case organization
sections.title: Sort evidence before choosing a mechanism
paragraphs: An integrated case may contain anatomical imaging, hormone concentrations, gamete evidence, developmental timing, exposure context, and technology outcomes. Sort each observation by scale—molecular, cellular, tissue, organ, whole-body, or population—and by sequence. This prevents a late outcome from being used as proof of an early cause.
Create an evidence ledger with observation, source, units, timing, reliability, and pathway relevance. Keep inferred events in a separate column from directly measured values.

sections.label: Competing explanations
sections.title: A good model must survive comparison
paragraphs: Generate at least two plausible explanations that make different predictions. For example, low downstream hormone response could reflect low signal, receptor difference, timing, or measurement context. A transport problem can coexist with normal gamete production. An exposure association can coexist with confounding. The strongest explanation fits multiple independent observations with the fewest unsupported additions.
A discriminating test is one expected to differ between alternatives. Repeating a measurement may improve reliability but will not always distinguish mechanisms.

sections.label: Developmental reasoning
sections.title: Sequence constrains what can cause what
paragraphs: Fertilization precedes cleavage, blastocyst formation, implantation, gastrulation, organogenesis, fetal growth, parturition, and lactation. Hormone sources and targets also change over time. A proposed mechanism cannot explain an event that occurred before the mechanism existed, and evidence from one stage should not be projected across every later stage.
Use a timeline to test temporal plausibility and identify missing evidence. Correct sequence is necessary for causation but is not sufficient by itself.

sections.label: Decision communication
sections.title: Recommendations should be about evidence steps
paragraphs: In an educational case, a recommendation should identify what to measure, compare, verify, or discuss next—not prescribe treatment or decide a person’s reproductive choices. Include scientific benefit, uncertainty, risk, access, consent, privacy, and affected perspectives. State how new evidence would change the conclusion.
A high-quality final explanation can remain provisional. Confidence should come from convergence and transparent limits rather than certainty language.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to connect chromosome structure, ploidy, DNA replication, and cell-cycle stages.
successCriteria: I can distinguish chromatin, a replicated chromosome, a chromatid, a homologous pair, and a chromosome set.
I can track DNA amount and chromosome number without counting chromatids as separate chromosomes.
I can explain how checkpoints connect growth conditions and DNA integrity to division.
C.materials: Chromosome-state model, centromere-count guide, DNA-amount table, and the Investigation Notebook.
C.safety: Use the supplied model chromosomes and synthetic cell records only. Chromosome counts in this lesson describe model cells and cannot diagnose a person or establish an individual health outcome.

warmup.title: Count by centromeres
warmup.prompt: A chromosome replicates into two sister chromatids. Has the chromosome number doubled? Explain the counting rule.
warmup.placeholder: State the centromere count, DNA amount, and chromosome number.

sections.label: Information package
sections.title: Chromosomes organize long DNA molecules
paragraphs: A eukaryotic chromosome is one DNA molecule with associated proteins before replication. Chromatin changes compaction across the cell cycle. Genes occupy loci, while homologous chromosomes carry corresponding loci inherited from different parents. Homologues may carry different alleles and are not identical copies.
Name the level being counted. A chromosome count uses centromeres, DNA amount reflects replication, and a homologous-pair count describes chromosome sets.

sections.label: Ploidy
sections.title: Chromosome sets and DNA copies are different quantities
paragraphs: Diploid cells contain two homologous chromosome sets, while haploid cells contain one. Replication doubles DNA and creates sister chromatids but does not change ploidy. Fertilization combines two haploid sets, and meiosis reduces a diploid lineage to haploid products.
Use n for chromosome sets only when the organism and stage are clear. Avoid using n as a substitute for total DNA amount.

sections.label: Cell cycle
sections.title: Interphase is active preparation
paragraphs: G1 includes growth and normal cell activity, S phase copies DNA, and G2 includes further preparation and repair before M phase. Cells can also enter non-dividing states. Interphase is not cellular rest; transcription, metabolism, growth, replication, and checkpoint control occur there.
A pulse-labelled DNA precursor appears mainly in S-phase cells. Cell counts across phases can estimate relative duration only when sampling assumptions are met.

sections.label: Control
sections.title: Checkpoints reduce propagation of damage
paragraphs: Checkpoint systems integrate DNA damage, replication completion, chromosome attachment, cell size, and external growth signals. Cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases, tumour suppressors, repair pathways, and programmed cell death contribute to regulation. Cancer can involve multiple accumulated changes rather than one universal switch.
A checkpoint delay is evidence that progression changed; it does not identify the exact molecule without targeted measurements.

conceptMap.title: Chromosome state across the cell cycle
conceptMap.description: An unreplicated chromosome is copied in S phase, sister chromatids remain joined, and segregation later distributes chromosome copies to daughter nuclei.

nodes.label: Before S
nodes.detail: One chromatid per chromosome; diploid set count is unchanged.

nodes.label: After S
nodes.detail: Two sister chromatids per chromosome and doubled DNA amount.

nodes.label: After division
nodes.detail: Each daughter nucleus receives one chromatid copy of each chromosome.

interaction.title: Chromosome-count evidence model
interaction.intro: Compare cells with the same ploidy but different DNA amounts.
interaction.prompt: Choose a case and report chromosome number, chromatid state, and ploidy separately.

cases.label: G1 model
cases.evidence: A diploid model cell has 8 centromeres and each chromosome contains one chromatid.
cases.explanation: The cell has 8 chromosomes, 8 chromatids, and two chromosome sets.

cases.label: G2 model
cases.evidence: The same cell has copied its DNA; 8 centromeres connect 16 sister chromatids.
cases.explanation: The cell still has 8 chromosomes and remains diploid, while DNA and chromatid number have doubled.

cases.label: Gamete model
cases.evidence: A mature model gamete contains 4 unreplicated chromosomes.
cases.explanation: The gamete is haploid because it contains one set; chromosome and chromatid counts are both 4 in this stage.

interaction.staticFallback: Count centromeres for chromosomes, count chromatids for DNA copies, and identify sets for ploidy.

practiceSeeds.prompt: Which event changes DNA amount without changing ploidy?
practiceSeeds.correct: DNA replication during S phase
distractors: Separation of homologues in meiosis I
Fertilization
Fusion of two nuclei
practiceSeeds.rationale: S phase creates sister chromatids while the number of chromosome sets remains the same. The correct statement identifies the relevant structure, signal, process, or evidence without adding a claim the lesson cannot support.
misconceptionFeedback: “Separation of homologues in meiosis I” is not supported. This assigns the mechanism, structure, or signal incorrectly. S phase creates sister chromatids while the number of chromosome sets remains the same.
“Fertilization” is not supported. This misses an important change in timing, location, or biological level. S phase creates sister chromatids while the number of chromosome sets remains the same.

“Fusion of two nuclei” is not supported. This turns a bounded relationship into a rule that the evidence does not support. S phase creates sister chromatids while the number of chromosome sets remains the same.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to explain how mitosis and cytokinesis produce two genetically equivalent nuclei and cells.
successCriteria: I can sequence prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, and cytokinesis by chromosome evidence.
I can explain spindle attachment and sister-chromatid separation without saying chromosomes choose where to move.
I can compare plant and animal cytokinesis and state what genetic equivalence does not mean.
C.materials: Mitosis evidence sequencer, chromosome-and-spindle model, plant and animal cytokinesis comparison, and the Investigation Notebook.
C.safety: Use the supplied cell images and descriptions; no stains, cultures, or live specimens are required. Stage evidence in a classroom model cannot diagnose abnormal growth in a person.

warmup.title: Equivalent is not unchanged
warmup.prompt: How can daughter cells be genetically equivalent yet later develop different structures or functions?
warmup.placeholder: Separate inherited DNA sequence from later gene expression and environment.

sections.label: Preparation
sections.title: Chromosomes condense and the spindle forms
paragraphs: During prophase and prometaphase, replicated chromosomes condense, centrosome-associated microtubules organize a spindle, the nuclear envelope breaks down, and kinetochores become accessible. Each sister chromatid has a kinetochore associated with its centromere region.
Stage labels summarize continuous changes. Identify a stage from several observations rather than one memorized picture.

sections.label: Alignment
sections.title: Metaphase tests bi-orientation
paragraphs: At metaphase, replicated chromosomes align near the cell equator. Sister kinetochores should connect to opposite spindle poles. The spindle-assembly checkpoint delays anaphase until attachments support balanced segregation.
A chromosome at the equator is not waiting by intention; forces and checkpoint signalling emerge from microtubule-kinetochore interactions.

sections.label: Separation
sections.title: Sister chromatids become daughter chromosomes
paragraphs: At anaphase, cohesion between sister chromatids is released. Kinetochore microtubules shorten and spindle geometry changes, moving daughter chromosomes toward opposite poles. Once sisters separate, each chromatid is counted as an independent chromosome.
Track centromeres before and after separation to avoid saying chromosome number disappears or permanently doubles.

sections.label: Completion
sections.title: Nuclei reform and the cytoplasm divides
paragraphs: Telophase includes chromosome decondensation and nuclear-envelope reformation. Cytokinesis divides cytoplasm. Animal cells commonly use an actin-myosin contractile ring and cleavage furrow; plant cells assemble vesicles into a cell plate that becomes new wall and membrane structures.
Genetic equivalence means the intended chromosome complement is copied, not that mutations never occur or that daughter cells must express the same genes forever.

conceptMap.title: Mitosis mechanism
conceptMap.description: Replicated chromosomes attach to a bipolar spindle, align, separate sister chromatids, reform nuclei, and divide the cytoplasm.

nodes.label: Attach
nodes.detail: Kinetochores connect sister chromatids to opposite poles.

nodes.label: Separate
nodes.detail: Cohesion release permits daughter chromosomes to move apart.

nodes.label: Partition
nodes.detail: Nuclei reform and cytokinesis creates two cells.

interaction.title: Mitosis evidence sequencer
interaction.intro: Identify stages from chromosome, spindle, and membrane evidence.
interaction.prompt: Choose a micrograph description and justify its stage.

cases.label: Aligned chromosomes
cases.evidence: Condensed duplicated chromosomes form one equatorial line with bipolar attachments.
cases.explanation: The evidence fits metaphase after attachment and before sister separation.

cases.label: Two moving groups
cases.evidence: Centromeres have separated and V-shaped daughter chromosomes move toward opposite poles.
cases.explanation: The defining evidence is sister-chromatid separation, so the stage is anaphase.

cases.label: Cell partition
cases.evidence: Two nuclei are visible while a plant cell plate grows across the centre.
cases.explanation: The nuclei have reformed and plant cytokinesis is partitioning the cytoplasm.

interaction.staticFallback: Use chromosome state, spindle relation, nuclear envelope, and cell-partition evidence for each stage.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to investigate cell-cycle timing and connect regulation evidence to cancer without reducing cancer to one cause.
successCriteria: I can estimate a mitotic index from counted cells and explain the sampling assumptions.
I can distinguish correlation, checkpoint mechanism, and causal evidence.
I can explain cancer as evolving cell populations with multiple possible regulatory changes.
C.materials: Synthetic cell-count dataset, mitotic-index calculator, graph grid, sampling checklist, and the Investigation Notebook.
C.safety: All tissue and tumour data are synthetic instructional data. Do not use mitotic index or classroom cell counts to infer a diagnosis, prognosis, or personal cancer risk.

warmup.title: A snapshot can estimate time
warmup.prompt: Why can the fraction of cells observed in mitosis estimate relative phase duration only under particular assumptions?
warmup.placeholder: Name sampling, steady-state, and cell-loss assumptions.

sections.label: Investigation
sections.title: Cell counts become a mitotic index
paragraphs: A mitotic index is the proportion of sampled cells visibly in mitosis: mitotic cells divided by total counted cells. In a large, asynchronously dividing, approximately steady population, a larger phase fraction can suggest more time spent in that phase. Sampling location and cell identification strongly affect the estimate.

Report raw counts, calculation, tissue region, classification rules, uncertainty, and repeated fields. A high index can reflect faster entry, slower mitosis, altered cell loss, or selection of an actively growing region.

sections.label: Regulation
sections.title: Cell-cycle control integrates positive and negative signals
paragraphs: Cyclin-CDK activity promotes transitions, while checkpoint proteins, DNA repair, growth-factor pathways, contact conditions, and programmed cell death can delay or stop progression. Tumour suppressors and proto-oncogenes describe normal regulatory roles; mutations can reduce restraints or create inappropriate growth signals.
One gene does not control every cancer. Different tissues and tumours can reach uncontrolled growth through different combinations and sequences of change.

sections.label: Cancer evolution
sections.title: Tumours are changing cell populations
paragraphs: Cells within a tumour can differ genetically and phenotypically. Variants that survive, proliferate, avoid immune removal, obtain resources, invade, or resist treatment may become more common. This somatic evolution helps explain heterogeneity, progression, and treatment resistance.
A mutation found in a tumour can be a driver, a passenger, or a later consequence. Frequency, timing, function, and experimental evidence help distinguish roles.

sections.label: Responsible claims
sections.title: Cell models do not diagnose a person
paragraphs: Microscope counts and cultured-cell evidence can test mechanisms but do not establish a diagnosis or treatment plan. Cancer risk and outcome depend on tissue, inherited and acquired variants, exposure, age, immune context, screening, access to care, and many other factors.
Use current authoritative sources and person-centred language. Avoid implying that cancer reflects a personal failure to regulate cells or make correct choices.

conceptMap.title: Cell-cycle investigation chain
conceptMap.description: Sampled cells are classified, a mitotic index is calculated, regulatory mechanisms are compared, and limits are used to bound the cancer inference.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to explain why meiosis uses two divisions after one DNA replication to produce haploid cells and variation.
successCriteria: I can distinguish homologous chromosomes from sister chromatids at every meiotic stage.
I can trace chromosome sets and DNA amount through meiosis I and II.
I can explain independent assortment and crossing over as different sources of variation.
C.materials: Meiosis chromosome model, homolog-and-chromatid tokens, variation evidence table, and the Investigation Notebook.
C.safety: This is a model-based investigation; no human gametes or biological samples are collected. Meiotic probabilities do not predict one person’s reproductive outcome.

warmup.title: What must be reduced?
warmup.prompt: Why must a diploid germ-cell lineage reduce chromosome sets before fertilization?
warmup.placeholder: Connect haploid gametes, diploid zygote, and stable chromosome number.

sections.label: Pairing
sections.title: Prophase I brings homologues together
paragraphs: After one S phase, homologous chromosomes pair through synapsis during prophase I. A paired structure contains four chromatids. Non-sister chromatids can exchange corresponding DNA segments through crossing over at chiasmata, producing recombinant chromatids.
Crossing over does not swap whole genes randomly or occur between arbitrary chromosomes; aligned homologous regions are exchanged.

sections.label: First division
sections.title: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes
paragraphs: At metaphase I, homologous pairs orient at the equator. Each pair can orient independently of other pairs. During anaphase I, homologues move to opposite poles while sister chromatids usually remain joined. The division reduces chromosome sets from diploid to haploid.
Independent assortment describes orientation of homologous pairs, while crossing over changes chromosome segments. Do not treat the mechanisms as synonyms.

sections.label: Second division
sections.title: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids
paragraphs: No new DNA replication occurs between meiosis I and II. Chromosomes align individually at metaphase II, and sister chromatids separate during anaphase II. The final products are haploid, but they are not necessarily genetically identical because of assortment, crossing over, and earlier mutation.
Track sets and DNA copies separately: cells are haploid after meiosis I even though chromosomes still have sister chromatids.

sections.label: Outcome
sections.title: Meiosis and fertilization form a chromosome-number cycle
paragraphs: Meiosis reduces chromosome sets, and fertilization restores diploidy by combining two haploid gametes. This cycle supports stable species chromosome number across generations while producing new allele combinations. Errors in pairing, recombination, attachment, or segregation can change chromosome content.
A meiotic error is probabilistic and stage-specific; it does not guarantee fertilization or one developmental outcome.

conceptMap.title: Meiotic reduction pathway
conceptMap.description: Homologues pair and recombine, meiosis I separates chromosome sets, meiosis II separates sister chromatids, and haploid products carry varied chromosome combinations.

nodes.label: Pair and recombine
nodes.detail: Homologues synapse and non-sister chromatids may exchange DNA.

nodes.label: Reduce
nodes.detail: Homologues separate in meiosis I, reducing ploidy.

nodes.label: Separate copies
nodes.detail: Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II without another S phase.

interaction.title: Meiosis chromosome tracker
interaction.intro: Inspect three stages of one model homologous pair.
interaction.prompt: Choose a stage and report homologue, chromatid, set, and variation evidence.

cases.label: Prophase I
cases.evidence: Replicated maternal and paternal homologues are synapsed and one chiasma is visible.
cases.explanation: The tetrad supports pairing and possible recombination between non-sister chromatids.

cases.label: After meiosis I
cases.evidence: Each daughter cell contains one replicated homologue from the original pair.
cases.explanation: The cells are haploid even though each chromosome still has sister chromatids.

cases.label: After meiosis II
cases.evidence: Four cells each contain one unreplicated chromosome from the pair, with two recombinant chromatids among them.
cases.explanation: Sister separation produced haploid products whose alleles differ because recombination occurred earlier.

interaction.staticFallback: Draw the pair at each stage and label chromosome sets, chromatids, and exchanged segments.
