sections.label: Spermatogenesis
sections.title: A continuing lineage produces many small gametes
paragraphs: After puberty, spermatogonial lineages can produce primary spermatocytes that enter meiosis. Meiosis I forms secondary spermatocytes, meiosis II forms spermatids, and later differentiation produces sperm. Cytoplasm is divided relatively evenly, supporting four potential meiotic products from one primary spermatocyte.
Sperm differentiation after meiosis changes shape and function but does not add another chromosome-reduction division.

sections.label: Oogenesis
sections.title: A finite lineage includes long meiotic pauses
paragraphs: Primary oocytes begin meiosis before birth and pause in prophase I. Selected cells resume meiosis after puberty. Completion of meiosis I produces a large secondary oocyte and a small polar body. The secondary oocyte typically pauses in metaphase II and completes meiosis II only after fertilization.
Cell name should match meiotic state. An ovulated secondary oocyte has not ordinarily completed meiosis II.

sections.label: Cytoplasm
sections.title: Unequal division preserves resources in one cell
paragraphs: Oogenesis allocates most cytoplasm, organelles, and stored molecules to one large cell, while polar bodies receive chromosome sets with little cytoplasm. Spermatogenesis prioritizes many motile cells with less cytoplasm. These are different reproductive strategies, not evidence that one gamete contributes more genetic value.
The zygote normally receives one haploid nuclear set from each gamete even though cytoplasmic contribution differs substantially.

sections.label: Age and error
sections.title: Timing changes the context for chromosome segregation
paragraphs: Oocytes may remain paused for years before completing meiosis, while sperm lineages continue dividing and renewing. Age-associated patterns and mutation sources therefore differ between pathways. Population-level probabilities do not determine one gamete or pregnancy outcome.
A nondisjunction pattern requires chromosome evidence; age alone is not a diagnosis or complete cause.

warmup.title: Variation or imbalance?
warmup.prompt: How can crossing over change allele combinations without changing chromosome number, while nondisjunction can change chromosome number?
warmup.placeholder: Compare exchanged segments with failed segregation.

sections.label: Crossing over
sections.title: Homologous exchange creates recombinant chromatids
paragraphs: During prophase I, aligned non-sister chromatids can break and rejoin at corresponding regions. Reciprocal exchange can produce new combinations of alleles on the same chromosome without adding or removing entire chromosomes. The frequency of recombination depends partly on distance and chromosome context.
A recombinant chromosome is not automatically abnormal. Recombination is a normal source of variation when exchange is balanced.

sections.label: Nondisjunction
sections.title: Segregation failure changes product chromosome content
paragraphs: If homologues fail to separate in meiosis I, all resulting products for that chromosome can have an extra or missing copy. If sister chromatids fail in meiosis II, two products may have typical copy number while one has an extra and one is missing a copy. Fertilization can then produce aneuploid zygotes.
Stage-specific product patterns help infer where segregation failed, but a single surviving cell may not reveal the complete event.

sections.label: Karyotypes
sections.title: Chromosome displays summarize large-scale evidence
paragraphs: A karyotype arranges stained metaphase chromosomes by size, centromere position, and banding pattern. It can reveal chromosome number and some large structural changes. It usually cannot show single-base variants, many small deletions, gene expression, receptor function, or every mosaic cell line.
Report what is visible: count, chromosome pair, and large pattern. Do not infer personality, worth, gender, or every health outcome.

sections.label: Ethics and communication
sections.title: Chromosome evidence carries privacy and uncertainty
paragraphs: Prenatal, diagnostic, or research chromosome testing involves consent, privacy, possible incidental findings, variable outcomes, and disability perspectives. The same chromosome pattern can be associated with a range of traits. Person-first or identity-first language should follow the preferences of affected communities and individuals.
A classroom karyotype is an instructional model, not clinical interpretation. Decisions require current professional guidance and respect for autonomy.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to compare reproductive life cycles and cell-division strategies by continuity, variation, speed, cost, and environmental context.
successCriteria: I can locate mitosis, meiosis, and fertilization in haploid-dominant, diploid-dominant, and alternation-of-generations models.
I can compare asexual and sexual reproduction without calling either universally superior.
I can evaluate cloning and telomere claims with current, qualified evidence.
C.materials: Local life-cycle diagrams, ploidy-transition markers, reproductive-strategy evidence board, and the Investigation Notebook.

warmup.title: Best under which conditions?
warmup.prompt: Why might a reproductive strategy be advantageous in one environment and costly in another?
warmup.placeholder: Compare speed, variation, mate requirement, resource use, and change.

sections.label: Life cycles
sections.title: Mitosis and meiosis occur at different ploidy transitions
paragraphs: In a diploid-dominant life cycle, meiosis produces haploid gametes and fertilization restores diploidy. In a haploid-dominant cycle, the zygote undergoes meiosis and much of the organism is haploid. Alternation of generations includes multicellular haploid and diploid stages connected by fertilization and meiosis.
Track ploidy at every arrow. Do not assume meiosis always directly produces gametes in every lineage.

sections.label: Asexual reproduction
sections.title: Mitosis can rapidly preserve a successful genotype
paragraphs: Asexual strategies can produce offspring without gamete fusion and may support rapid colonization when conditions are stable. Offspring are genetically similar to the parent except for mutation and other changes. Low recombination can limit the generation of new combinations when environments or pathogens change.
Similarity is not perfect identity, and low variation is not always disadvantageous. Fitness depends on the current environment.

sections.label: Sexual reproduction
sections.title: Recombination can create diverse combinations at a cost
paragraphs: Sexual reproduction combines meiosis and fertilization, creating variation through assortment, crossing over, and random gamete union. Costs may include finding mates, specialized structures, slower reproduction, and passing only part of one genome to each offspring. Benefits depend on ecological and evolutionary context.
Avoid framing sexual reproduction as an automatic ladder of progress. Both strategies persist because tradeoffs vary.

sections.label: Cloning claims
sections.title: A clone is not a replay of one organism
paragraphs: Cloning by embryo splitting or nuclear transfer can produce a nuclear genome closely related to a donor, but mitochondrial DNA, epigenetic state, prenatal environment, development, and experience can differ. Early claims that one cloned animal’s telomeres proved universal premature aging were oversimplified; cloning outcomes vary and reprogramming is incomplete.
A clone is not genetically or personally identical in every respect, and one animal cannot establish a universal lifespan rule.

warmup.title: Invisible factors from visible ratios
warmup.prompt: How could repeated offspring ratios reveal something about hereditary factors that could not be seen directly?
warmup.placeholder: Connect controlled crosses, counts, predictions, and alternative models.

sections.label: Experimental design
sections.title: Controlled crosses isolate inheritance patterns
paragraphs: Mendel used pea varieties with contrasting traits, controlled pollination, and counted many offspring across generations. True-breeding parental lines produced uniform F1 patterns for selected traits, while F2 generations revealed reappearance of alternatives. Replication and large counts made the ratios informative.
The historical model was powerful because the organisms and traits fit it well. It should not be transferred uncritically to every human or continuous trait.

sections.label: Alleles
sections.title: A gene can have alternative sequence forms
paragraphs: A gene occupies a locus, and alleles are alternative versions at that locus. In a diploid organism, two homologues can carry the same allele or different alleles. Homozygous and heterozygous describe genotype at a locus, while phenotype describes an observed trait under particular genetic and environmental conditions.
Dominant means expressed in a heterozygote under the model; it does not mean common, healthy, strong, desirable, or likely to increase.

sections.label: Segregation
sections.title: Allele pairs separate when homologues separate
paragraphs: The law of segregation states that two alleles in a diploid individual separate into different gametes. The chromosome mechanism is separation of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I, followed by distribution into haploid products. Fertilization pairs one allele from each contributing gamete source.
A Punnett square represents gamete probabilities and combinations, not a physical movement of letters or a guaranteed family ratio.

sections.label: Model boundaries
sections.title: One-gene models are deliberately simplified
paragraphs: Mendelian ratios can be altered by small samples, linkage, incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, penetrance, environmental influence, viability differences, meiotic drive, or scoring error. A model remains useful when its assumptions and limits are explicit.
Select examples with validated inheritance. Avoid textbook claims that tongue rolling, attached earlobes, eye colour, or many other complex human traits are single-gene binaries.

conceptMap.title: Segregation evidence chain
conceptMap.description: Diploid organisms carry allele pairs, homologues separate in meiosis, gametes carry one allele, and fertilization creates genotype probabilities.

nodes.label: Pair
nodes.detail: Two homologues can carry same or different alleles.

nodes.label: Segregate
nodes.detail: Homologue separation places one allele copy into a gamete.

nodes.label: Combine
nodes.detail: Random gamete union creates offspring genotype probabilities.

interaction.title: Mendelian ratio interpreter

cases.evidence: A monohybrid F2 sample of 1,200 offspring is close to a 3:1 phenotype ratio.
cases.explanation: The large sample is consistent with the simple dominance and segregation model, while consistency is not proof that no alternative exists.

cases.label: Small sample
cases.evidence: A family-sized sample of four offspring shows four dominant phenotypes.
cases.explanation: The outcome is possible under a 3:1 probability and does not show that segregation failed.

cases.label: Consistent departure
cases.evidence: Repeated large crosses show a stable ratio far from the Mendelian prediction.
cases.explanation: The pattern justifies testing linkage, viability, scoring, penetrance, or another model assumption.

warmup.placeholder: Connect meiosis, allele segregation, and conditional probability.

sections.label: Model setup
sections.title: Define the inheritance model before calculating
paragraphs: A monohybrid cross follows one locus. State allele symbols, dominance relation, parental genotypes, and the phenotype-genotype link. Use uppercase and lowercase only as labels; letters do not make one allele stronger. The example must have evidence for the assumed inheritance pattern.
A correct grid built on an incorrect model still produces a misleading answer. Record assumptions before arithmetic.

sections.label: Gamete derivation
sections.title: Each gamete receives one allele copy
paragraphs: A heterozygous diploid Aa produces A-bearing and a-bearing gametes under the simple segregation model, commonly at equal probability. A homozygous AA parent produces only A-bearing gametes for the locus. List gamete types and probabilities along the grid axes.
The grid combines gametes; it does not show meiosis itself. Link the probabilities back to homologue separation.

sections.label: Combination
sections.title: Boxes represent equally likely unions only under stated assumptions
paragraphs: For Aa × Aa, the four combinations are AA, Aa, Aa, and aa, giving genotype probabilities 1/4, 1/2, and 1/4. With complete dominance, phenotype probabilities are 3/4 dominant and 1/4 recessive. Repeated boxes represent probability weight, not different genotypes.
Check that genotype probabilities sum to 1 and that phenotype categories include every genotype exactly once.

sections.label: Interpretation
sections.title: Each reproductive event is a new probability trial
paragraphs: A 1/4 probability does not mean every fourth child must have the phenotype or that previous outcomes change the next probability under the model. Small families can show many ratios. Probability supports counselling and prediction only when the inheritance model, parent genotypes, penetrance, and evidence are appropriate.
Avoid deterministic wording and remember that real human traits can involve multiple genes, environment, and incomplete information.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to use multiplication, addition, test crosses, and sampling evidence to evaluate inheritance probabilities.
successCriteria: I can choose multiplication for joint independent events and addition for mutually exclusive routes.
I can use a test cross to update an unknown genotype explanation.
I can compare observed and expected counts without assuming small deviations disprove a model.
C.materials: Probability-rule guide, synthetic test-cross datasets, expected-count calculator, and the Investigation Notebook.

warmup.title: And or either?
warmup.prompt: When should probabilities be multiplied, and when should they be added in a genetics problem?
warmup.placeholder: Give one joint-event and one mutually exclusive example.

sections.label: Probability rules
sections.title: Multiplication and addition answer different questions
paragraphs: For independent events that must both occur, multiply probabilities. For mutually exclusive routes that lead to the same outcome, add their probabilities. A heterozygote can arise through A from one parent and a from the other or the reverse route; the two route probabilities are added.
Write the event statement before the operation. Arithmetic without event definitions is difficult to audit.

sections.label: Test cross
sections.title: A recessive partner exposes an unknown allele contribution
paragraphs: An organism with a dominant phenotype may be AA or Aa in a complete-dominance model. Crossing with aa makes the predictions differ: AA × aa produces all Aa, while Aa × aa predicts half Aa and half aa. Offspring evidence changes confidence in the alternatives.
All dominant offspring in a small sample do not prove AA because the heterozygous model can produce that pattern by chance.

sections.label: Sampling variation
sections.title: Observed counts fluctuate around probability
paragraphs: Expected counts equal probability multiplied by sample size, but random segregation and fertilization create variation. Larger samples usually show smaller proportional deviations. Repeated departures can also reflect linkage, viability, scoring, non-random sampling, or an incorrect inheritance model.
Report observed and expected counts, sample size, direction and magnitude of departure, and whether a formal goodness-of-fit test is appropriate.

sections.label: Model revision
sections.title: Evidence updates rather than instantly proves
paragraphs: A test-cross result can make one genotype more plausible, but confidence depends on sample size, parentage, penetrance, scoring, and model validity. Scientific reasoning asks how likely the data are under each explanation and what next observation would discriminate.
Use probabilistic language such as “supports,” “is consistent with,” and “is less likely,” not “proves” when alternatives remain.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to model incomplete dominance, codominance, and multiple alleles without confusing phenotype expression with allele frequency or value.
successCriteria: I can distinguish complete dominance, incomplete dominance, and codominance by heterozygote evidence.
I can solve a multiple-allele problem while remembering that one individual carries at most two alleles at an autosomal locus.
I can select a model from evidence rather than forcing every trait into dominant-recessive notation.

warmup.title: Look at the heterozygote
warmup.prompt: What phenotype evidence would distinguish incomplete dominance from codominance?
warmup.placeholder: Describe blended/intermediate expression versus simultaneous distinct expression.

sections.label: Incomplete dominance
sections.title: The heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype
paragraphs: In incomplete dominance, neither allele produces the same heterozygote phenotype as either homozygote under the measured conditions. A red-flowered and white-flowered model can produce pink heterozygotes. The alleles themselves do not blend permanently; segregation can recover both homozygous phenotypes.
An F2 phenotype ratio can match 1:2:1 because each genotype has a distinguishable phenotype.

sections.label: Codominance
sections.title: Both allele products are detectably expressed
paragraphs: In codominance, heterozygotes show products associated with both alleles, as in AB blood-group antigen expression. Codominance does not mean every cell or molecule is half one and half another; it means both allele effects are detected in the defined phenotype.
Select the model from molecular or phenotype evidence, not from whether one trait sounds visually stronger.

sections.label: Multiple alleles
sections.title: Populations can contain more alleles than an individual
paragraphs: A locus can have several allele forms in a population. The ABO blood-group model includes IA, IB, and i, while a diploid individual ordinarily carries two. IA and IB are codominant to each other and each is dominant to i in the simplified antigen model.
Allele hierarchy must be stated explicitly. Blood type alone may not uniquely determine genotype for A or B phenotypes.

sections.label: Model choice
sections.title: Notation should preserve the biology
paragraphs: Superscripts or distinct symbols reduce the misleading implication that one allele is inherently superior. Before calculating, define allele products, heterozygote phenotype, genotype-phenotype map, and population scope. Environment and measurement method can still affect phenotype.
These models explain selected loci; they should not be generalized to complex human characteristics or social categories.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to solve dihybrid probability problems and explain when independent assortment is a valid assumption.
successCriteria: I can derive gametes for two unlinked loci using meiosis or probability.
I can calculate joint genotype or phenotype probabilities without relying only on a 16-box grid.
I can explain why linkage or other model violations change expected ratios.
C.materials: Two-locus gamete table, probability tree, dihybrid-grid template, calculator, and the Investigation Notebook.

warmup.title: Two loci, one gamete

sections.label: Independent assortment
sections.title: Homologous pairs orient independently in meiosis I
paragraphs: When loci are on different chromosome pairs—or effectively unlinked—the orientation of one homologous pair does not determine another. An AaBb parent then produces AB, Ab, aB, and ab gametes with equal probability under the simple model.
Independent assortment is a chromosome-behaviour assumption, not a statement that every gene in a genome is independent.

sections.label: Branch method
sections.title: Multiply locus probabilities for joint outcomes
paragraphs: A dihybrid cross can be decomposed into two monohybrid crosses when loci assort independently. For AaBb × AaBb, the probability of aa is 1/4 and bb is 1/4, so aabb is 1/16. The method reduces grid errors and makes assumptions visible.
Use addition when several mutually exclusive genotype routes produce the same requested phenotype.

sections.label: Grid method
sections.title: A 4-by-4 grid represents sixteen gamete unions
paragraphs: Listing four gametes from each heterozygous parent yields sixteen equally weighted boxes under the model. With complete dominance at both loci, phenotype classes can form a 9:3:3:1 ratio. That ratio depends on segregation, independent assortment, dominance, equal viability, and adequate sample size.
Do not memorize 9:3:3:1 without connecting it to gamete probabilities and assumptions.

sections.label: Departures
sections.title: Linkage and sampling change observed patterns
paragraphs: Genes on the same chromosome can be inherited together more often than predicted by independence, especially when close. Recombination can still produce non-parental combinations. Small samples fluctuate, and viability or scoring can also alter ratios.
A ratio departure is evidence to investigate, not automatic proof of linkage. Compare reciprocal classes, recombination, sample size, and alternative explanations.

sections.label: Chromosome context
sections.title: Sex-linked loci travel with sex chromosomes
paragraphs: An X-linked locus is located on the X chromosome. A person with one X has one allele copy at many X-linked loci, while a person with two X chromosomes can carry two. Y-linked loci pass through Y-chromosome inheritance. Chromosomal and developmental variation means classroom categories are simplified.
Use karyotype and inheritance context stated in the fictional case. Do not infer gender identity from pedigree symbols or chromosome assumptions.

sections.label: X-linked model
sections.title: Recessive expression depends on allele context
paragraphs: In a simplified X-linked recessive model, a person with one X carrying the allele can express the phenotype because no second allele at the locus is present. A heterozygous person with two X chromosomes may be described as a carrier, though X-inactivation, penetrance, and phenotype definition can affect expression.
Use superscript notation and include chromosome contribution from each gamete source.

sections.label: Pedigree clues
sections.title: Patterns support alternatives rather than one magic rule
paragraphs: X-linked recessive patterns may show more affected people with one X and no father-to-son transmission under the simplified model. Autosomal patterns can affect sexes similarly, while mitochondrial inheritance follows the egg lineage. Small pedigrees, missing people, uncertain parentage, variable penetrance, and new mutation can obscure patterns.
No single affected individual establishes the inheritance mode. Compare the whole pedigree and list genotypes as known, possible, or excluded.

sections.label: Ethics
sections.title: Family genetic evidence is private and relational
paragraphs: A result can reveal information about biological relatives who did not choose testing. Pedigree analysis can also intersect with adoption, donor conception, misattributed parentage, and cultural definitions of family. Classroom work must use fictional pedigrees and avoid collecting real family health histories.
Clinical interpretation requires consent, counselling, validated testing, and respectful communication of uncertainty.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to use recombination frequency as evidence for gene linkage and relative chromosome-map distance.
successCriteria: I can identify parental and recombinant classes in a test cross.
I can calculate recombination frequency and map units with a clear denominator.
I can explain why two-point data underestimate long distances and do not uniquely establish gene order.
C.materials: Synthetic recombinant-offspring table, chromosome-map scale, recombination calculator, and the Investigation Notebook.
C.safety: Use the supplied model-organism data only. Recombination frequency estimates relative map distance; it does not reveal identity, ancestry, or an exact physical distance in every cross.

warmup.title: A map from offspring
warmup.prompt: How can offspring phenotype counts provide evidence about the distance between genes on a chromosome?
warmup.placeholder: Connect crossing over, recombinant gametes, and frequency.

sections.label: Linkage
sections.title: Genes on one chromosome can travel together
paragraphs: Loci on the same chromosome are linked, but crossing over can create recombinant chromatids. Close loci have fewer opportunities for a crossover between them than loci farther apart. In a test cross, offspring classes can reveal gamete types from the heterozygous parent.
The most frequent classes are often parental and smaller reciprocal classes recombinant, assuming viability and scoring do not bias counts.

sections.label: Calculation
sections.title: Recombination frequency estimates relative distance
paragraphs: Recombination frequency equals recombinant offspring divided by total offspring, multiplied by 100 percent. One percent recombination is defined as approximately one map unit or centimorgan. Show both reciprocal recombinant classes and use the full sample denominator.
A map unit is a statistical distance, not an exact physical base-pair length that is constant across species or chromosome regions.

sections.label: Limits
sections.title: Observed recombination cannot exceed fifty percent
paragraphs: Multiple crossovers can restore a parental arrangement and go undetected in a two-point cross. Widely separated loci therefore approach 50 percent recombination and can appear unlinked. Recombination rates also vary by sex, species, chromosome region, and biological context.
Two-point frequency estimates order poorly over long intervals. Three-point crosses or molecular markers provide stronger mapping evidence.

sections.label: Gene order
sections.title: Three loci require comparison of crossover classes
paragraphs: In a three-point test cross, largest classes are often parental and smallest classes double crossovers. Comparing allele arrangement between these classes can identify the middle gene. Distances are estimated for adjacent intervals and checked against observed double-crossovers.
Gene order is an inference from class patterns and assumptions. Label synthetic data and test for viability or scoring effects before concluding.

I can evaluate genetic information through evidence, uncertainty, privacy, equity, and informed consent.

C.safety: Use aggregate, non-identifying data. Do not treat race, ancestry, disability, achievement, behaviour, or personal worth as genetically fixed categories, and do not infer an individual outcome from a group trend.

warmup.title: Beyond two boxes
warmup.prompt: Why do height, many health risks, and numerous physiological measurements form continuous distributions rather than simple dominant-recessive groups?
warmup.placeholder: Connect many loci, environment, development, and measurement.

sections.label: Polygenic inheritance
sections.title: Many loci can contribute small effects
paragraphs: A polygenic trait is influenced by variants at multiple loci. Additive models can produce many genotype combinations and a range of phenotypes, but real interactions may be non-additive. No single “tall gene,” “intelligence gene,” or “athletic gene” explains a complex human outcome.
A distribution can shift with allele frequencies while retaining substantial overlap. Group averages do not identify an individual genotype or ability.

sections.label: Environment and development
sections.title: Phenotype emerges through interaction
paragraphs: Nutrition, health, learning, stress, physical environment, social conditions, random developmental events, and measurement context can influence phenotype. Gene-environment interaction means a genetic effect can differ across environments; it does not mean genes and environment contribute separable fixed percentages to one person.
Heritability describes variation in a studied population and environment, not immutability, personal destiny, or the fraction of an individual caused by genes.

sections.label: Penetrance and expressivity
sections.title: The same variant may not produce one identical phenotype
paragraphs: Penetrance describes the proportion of people with a genotype who show a defined phenotype. Expressivity describes variation in degree or form among those who show it. Modifier genes, environment, age, sex-related biology, mosaicism, and measurement definitions can contribute.
A risk variant changes probability under defined evidence; it does not guarantee disease or absence of disease.

sections.label: Genetic decisions
sections.title: Information can help and harm
paragraphs: Genetic testing can support diagnosis, screening, reproductive planning, treatment selection, or research, while raising questions about validity, uncertain findings, privacy, family implications, discrimination, access, ancestry databases, data governance, and Indigenous data sovereignty. Benefits and harms depend on purpose and context.
A responsible brief asks whether the test is analytically valid, clinically meaningful, actionable, consented to, equitably accessible, and governed by affected people.

conceptMap.title: Complex-trait evidence pathway
conceptMap.description: Multiple loci interact with development and environment to produce a distribution; testing estimates selected probabilities and requires careful governance.

nodes.label: Combine influences
nodes.detail: Many variants and contexts contribute to phenotype.

nodes.label: Measure distribution
nodes.detail: Describe centre, spread, overlap, and population definition.

nodes.label: Decide responsibly
nodes.detail: Evaluate validity, uncertainty, consent, privacy, equity, and actionability.

warmup.title: A model constrained by evidence
warmup.prompt: What observations would a DNA model need to explain besides simply looking like a helix?
warmup.placeholder: Consider chemical composition, width, repetition, base ratios, and copying.

sections.label: Information molecule
sections.title: Evidence identified DNA as hereditary material
paragraphs: Transformation experiments showed that heritable information could move between bacterial cells. Work by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty supported DNA as the transforming principle, and Hershey-Chase bacteriophage evidence further distinguished DNA from protein in that system. These studies did not by themselves reveal molecular structure.
History is cumulative: each experiment answered a different question with particular organisms, methods, and limits.

sections.label: Chemical constraints
sections.title: Nucleotides form directional polymers
paragraphs: Each DNA nucleotide includes deoxyribose, phosphate, and a nitrogenous base. Phosphodiester bonds create a sugar-phosphate backbone with 5-prime to 3-prime direction. Chargaff’s base measurements showed approximate A=T and G=C relationships in double-stranded DNA while base composition varies among species.
Base ratios constrain pairing but do not alone prove a helix or explain strand orientation.

sections.label: Diffraction evidence
sections.title: Franklin and Wilkins produced structural constraints
paragraphs: Rosalind Franklin’s careful X-ray diffraction work, including the image known as Photo 51 produced with Raymond Gosling, provided evidence of helical regularity, dimensions, and phosphate placement. Maurice Wilkins also contributed diffraction work. Data access and credit occurred in an unequal historical context that should be represented accurately.
Diffraction patterns require mathematical and physical interpretation; they are evidence, not a direct photograph of a DNA molecule.

sections.label: Double-helix model
sections.title: Complementary antiparallel strands explain copying
paragraphs: Watson and Crick assembled a model consistent with chemical and diffraction constraints: two antiparallel strands, sugar-phosphate backbones outward, and complementary base pairs inward. A-T and G-C pairing provides consistent width and a mechanism for templated copying. Later evidence refined DNA forms, dynamics, protein interactions, and chromatin organization.
Scientific models are credited through the evidence network, not only the final published structure.

conceptMap.title: DNA model evidence convergence
conceptMap.description: Hereditary evidence identifies DNA, chemistry constrains nucleotides and base ratios, diffraction constrains shape and dimensions, and model building integrates the findings.

nodes.label: Identify function
nodes.detail: Transformation and phage evidence support DNA as hereditary material.

nodes.label: Constrain structure
nodes.detail: Chemistry, base ratios, and diffraction restrict viable models.

nodes.label: Integrate and test
nodes.detail: The antiparallel double helix predicts complementary templating and further evidence.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to explain semiconservative DNA replication as coordinated unwinding, priming, synthesis, proofreading, and joining.
successCriteria: I can identify the roles of helicase, single-strand-binding proteins, primase, DNA polymerase, and ligase.
I can explain leading and lagging synthesis from antiparallel templates.
I can use evidence to distinguish replication error, repair, and inherited mutation.

C.safety: Use the local molecular model and synthetic sequences only. No microbial culture, radioactive label, chemical reagent, or personal DNA sample is required.

warmup.title: One direction on opposite templates
warmup.prompt: If DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to a 3-prime end, why must the two new strands be synthesized differently at a replication fork?
warmup.placeholder: Connect antiparallel templates and fork direction.

sections.label: Semiconservative model
sections.title: Each daughter molecule keeps one parental strand
paragraphs: Replication begins at origins and proceeds through forks. Helicase separates base pairs, topological strain is managed, and single-strand-binding proteins stabilize exposed templates. Each parental strand guides a complementary new strand, producing daughter molecules with one old and one new strand.
Semiconservative replication was tested with isotope-density evidence; complementarity alone suggested but did not prove the model.

sections.label: Initiation
sections.title: Polymerase requires a primer and a template
paragraphs: Primase synthesizes short RNA primers that provide a free 3-prime hydroxyl. DNA polymerases extend from primers by adding complementary deoxyribonucleotides in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction. Base-pair geometry and enzyme active sites support fidelity.
Polymerase does not begin a strand from nothing and does not read the template in the same direction as synthesis.

sections.label: Two strands
sections.title: Leading and lagging synthesis solve antiparallel geometry
paragraphs: The leading strand can be synthesized continuously toward the moving fork on one template. The lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously away from the fork as Okazaki fragments. Primers are removed or replaced, and DNA ligase seals remaining backbone gaps.
Both strands are synthesized 5-prime to 3-prime. The labels describe relation to fork movement, not different chemical direction.

sections.label: Fidelity
sections.title: Proofreading and repair reduce—but do not eliminate—errors
paragraphs: Polymerase proofreading can remove some mismatched nucleotides, and additional repair systems inspect DNA. An unrepaired change becomes a mutation after it is fixed in a DNA molecule and propagated. Somatic and germ-line contexts differ in whether a variant can pass to offspring.
A DNA change can be neutral, harmful, or beneficial depending on location, cell, environment, and effect; mutation is not synonymous with disease.

conceptMap.title: Replication fork mechanism
conceptMap.description: DNA is unwound, primers provide starting points, polymerase extends complementary strands, lagging fragments are processed, and ligase completes the backbone.

nodes.label: Open and stabilize
nodes.detail: Helicase and associated proteins expose templates.

nodes.label: Prime and synthesize
nodes.detail: Polymerase extends 5-prime to 3-prime on leading and lagging strands.

nodes.label: Proofread and join
nodes.detail: Errors are corrected and fragment gaps are sealed.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to explain transcription as regulated RNA synthesis from one DNA template strand.
successCriteria: I can identify promoter, template strand, coding strand, RNA polymerase, transcript, and termination.
I can write an RNA sequence with correct complementarity and 5-prime/3-prime direction.
I can distinguish transcription, RNA processing, and translation in location and product.
C.materials: Transcription model, synthetic template and coding strands, RNA-processing evidence table, and the Investigation Notebook.
C.safety: All sequences are synthetic instructional data. Sequence interpretation here cannot diagnose disease, identify a person, or establish ancestry or biological relationships.

warmup.title: One gene, one template strand
warmup.prompt: Why is only one DNA strand used as the template for a particular transcript, even though both strands contain nucleotide sequences?
warmup.placeholder: Connect promoter orientation, polymerase direction, and RNA complementarity.

sections.label: Initiation
sections.title: Promoters orient RNA synthesis
paragraphs: Transcription begins when regulatory proteins and RNA polymerase assemble at a promoter. Promoter orientation determines which DNA strand is the template and where transcription starts. Gene regulation changes when, where, and how much RNA is produced; not every gene is transcribed in every cell.
A promoter is a DNA regulatory region, not part of the amino-acid sequence, and different genes use different regulatory contexts.

sections.label: Elongation
sections.title: RNA grows 5-prime to 3-prime
paragraphs: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template 3-prime to 5-prime and adds complementary ribonucleotides to the RNA 3-prime end. RNA uses uracil instead of thymine. The RNA sequence resembles the coding DNA strand except U replaces T, when both are written 5-prime to 3-prime.
Always label strand direction. Complementing a coding strand directly without considering orientation is a common error.

sections.label: Termination and processing
sections.title: A primary transcript can be modified
paragraphs: Termination signals end transcription. In eukaryotes, a primary pre-mRNA is processed through 5-prime capping, poly-A addition, and splicing that removes introns and joins exons. Alternative splicing can produce different mature RNAs from one gene under regulated conditions.
Introns are not simply useless DNA, and one gene does not always equal one protein product.

sections.label: Regulation and evidence
sections.title: RNA abundance is a snapshot of expression
paragraphs: Measuring RNA can reveal which genes are transcribed in a sample, but RNA abundance also reflects degradation, cell composition, timing, and method. It does not automatically establish protein amount or activity because translation and protein turnover add later regulation.
A cell-expression claim should name tissue, condition, time, reference genes, and measurement uncertainty.

conceptMap.title: Transcription pathway
conceptMap.description: Regulatory signals recruit polymerase, one DNA strand templates 5-prime-to-3-prime RNA synthesis, and processing creates a mature transcript.

nodes.label: Initiate
nodes.detail: Promoter orientation selects start site and template strand.

nodes.label: Elongate
nodes.detail: RNA polymerase adds complementary RNA nucleotides.

nodes.label: Process
nodes.detail: Capping, polyadenylation, and splicing produce mature eukaryotic mRNA.

cases.label: Splice variant

cases.explanation: Alternative splicing produced distinct mature transcripts from the same gene region.

cases.label: RNA-protein mismatch
cases.evidence: mRNA abundance rises, but protein abundance remains low.

sections.label: Genetic code
sections.title: Codons connect nucleotide sequence to amino acids
paragraphs: The genetic code uses three-nucleotide mRNA codons. AUG commonly establishes a start codon and specifies methionine, while UAA, UAG, and UGA serve as stop signals in the standard code. The code is redundant because several codons can specify the same amino acid, but it is not ambiguous within the standard table.
Read the mRNA 5-prime to 3-prime from the established start. A DNA sequence must first be identified as template or coding and converted correctly.

sections.label: tRNA and ribosome
sections.title: Adaptor molecules align amino acids with codons
paragraphs: Each charged tRNA carries an amino acid and presents an anticodon that base-pairs antiparallel with a codon. The ribosome positions tRNAs in A, P, and E sites and catalyzes peptide-bond formation through ribosomal RNA activity. The mRNA moves through the ribosome one codon at a time.
tRNA does not carry a DNA gene, and a ribosome does not decide which amino acid feels appropriate; molecular recognition drives the sequence.

sections.label: Initiation to termination
sections.title: Translation has ordered stages
paragraphs: Initiation assembles the small ribosomal subunit, mRNA, initiator tRNA, and large subunit at the start region. Elongation cycles add amino acids and move the ribosome. At a stop codon, release factors—not a stop tRNA—promote polypeptide release and complex disassembly.
A premature stop can shorten a polypeptide, but cellular consequences depend on transcript surveillance and protein context.

sections.label: Protein fate
sections.title: Sequence enters a larger folding and regulation system
paragraphs: A polypeptide can fold, combine with other subunits, be cleaved, acquire chemical modifications, and move to a specific cellular location. Chaperones and cellular conditions influence folding. Protein function depends on three-dimensional structure, interactions, amount, location, and timing.
A codon change may be synonymous, alter an amino acid, create a stop, affect splicing, or have no measurable phenotype. Sequence consequence is context-dependent.

conceptMap.title: Translation mechanism
conceptMap.description: A start codon sets the reading frame, tRNAs match codons, the ribosome forms peptide bonds, a stop releases the chain, and folding and modification shape function.

nodes.label: Elongate

nodes.label: Terminate and fold

successCriteria: I can distinguish substitution, insertion, deletion, frameshift, chromosomal, somatic, and germ-line changes.

C.materials: Mutation sequence cards, local codon table, synthetic tumour-variant dataset, evidence-ranking guide, and the Investigation Notebook.

warmup.title: Change is not consequence
warmup.prompt: Why can the same category of DNA change have very different effects depending on its location and cellular context?
warmup.placeholder: Connect coding, regulatory, splice, redundancy, protein structure, and cell lineage.

sections.label: Mutation types
sections.title: DNA changes vary in scale and location
paragraphs: A substitution changes one base pair; an insertion or deletion adds or removes sequence; non-multiple-of-three coding indels can shift a reading frame. Larger changes include duplications, inversions, translocations, copy-number changes, and chromosome-number differences. Mutations can arise from replication error, damage, repair, or mobile elements.
Classification describes the DNA event, not whether the outcome is beneficial, neutral, or harmful.

sections.label: Consequence pathway
sections.title: Most DNA change effects are filtered through context
paragraphs: A change outside coding sequence can affect regulation, splicing, chromosome organization, or have no measurable effect. Coding changes can be synonymous, missense, nonsense, or frameshifting. Protein effect depends on domain, chemistry, dosage, expression, interactions, and compensation.
Trace evidence level by level instead of jumping from DNA variant directly to a person’s phenotype.

sections.label: Lineage
sections.title: Somatic and germ-line mutations have different inheritance routes
paragraphs: A somatic mutation arises in a body-cell lineage and can be passed to its mitotic descendants but ordinarily not to offspring. A germ-line mutation can enter a gamete lineage and be inherited. Mosaicism occurs when cell populations within one organism differ genetically.
Tissue sample, variant fraction, and developmental timing help infer lineage; one blood sample may not represent every tissue.

sections.label: Cancer evidence
sections.title: Cancer can emerge through mutation and selection
paragraphs: Cancer often involves accumulated regulatory changes affecting proliferation, repair, death, genome stability, immune interaction, metabolism, and tissue invasion. Some variants drive growth; many passengers accompany expansion. Environmental exposures can change mutation rates or selection, while inherited variants can alter risk.
A tumour sequence is not a complete cause or prognosis. Interpretation needs matched tissue, function, frequency, tumour context, treatment evidence, and clinical expertise.

conceptMap.title: Mutation consequence pathway
conceptMap.description: A DNA change occurs in a genomic and cell-lineage context, may alter RNA or protein, changes cell behaviour if function is affected, and can be selected within tissues.

C.learningIntention: I am learning to explain how restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors, transformation, and selection support recombinant-DNA experiments.
successCriteria: I can trace DNA from source sequence through cutting, joining, introduction, and verification.
I can distinguish selectable marker, reporter, insert, vector, host cell, and expression evidence.
I can evaluate biotechnology benefit and risk without assuming that successful transformation guarantees correct expression or safety.
C.materials: Restriction-site map, recombinant-vector model, transformation-and-selection dataset, and the Investigation Notebook.
C.safety: This is a paper-and-screen model only. Do not culture organisms, handle recombinant material, use restriction enzymes, or perform an unsupervised wet-lab procedure.

warmup.title: Build and verify
warmup.prompt: Why is inserting DNA into a vector not enough to prove that a host cell contains the correct sequence and produces a functional protein?
warmup.placeholder: Add orientation, sequence, uptake, expression, folding, and verification.

sections.label: Restriction
sections.title: Sequence-specific enzymes cut DNA reproducibly
paragraphs: Restriction endonucleases recognize selected DNA sequences and cut phosphodiester backbones, producing sticky or blunt ends depending on the enzyme. Matching compatible ends can support controlled assembly. A recognition site can occur within an intended insert, so map design matters.
A restriction enzyme does not know which gene scientists want; it acts wherever its recognition and reaction conditions permit.

sections.label: Ligation and vectors
sections.title: A vector carries an assembled insert
paragraphs: DNA ligase seals compatible backbone breaks. Plasmid vectors can include an origin of replication, selectable marker, cloning site, regulatory elements, and inserted sequence. Insert orientation and reading frame matter when expression is intended.
A closed plasmid band or antibiotic-resistant colony does not by itself prove correct insert sequence, orientation, or function.

sections.label: Transformation and selection
sections.title: Cells must receive and retain the construct
paragraphs: Transformation introduces DNA into cells through method-specific processes. Selection allows cells with a marker to survive or be identified, while reporters can provide visible or measurable signals. Controls distinguish background growth, failed transformation, and construct-dependent effects.
Selection identifies a marker phenotype; it is not direct evidence for every part of the construct.

sections.label: Verification and STS
sections.title: Biotechnology claims need molecular and social evidence
paragraphs: Restriction analysis, PCR, sequencing, RNA measurement, protein assays, and functional tests answer different verification questions. Applications can include medicine, agriculture, research, and environmental work while raising issues of containment, off-target effects, access, ownership, consent, ecological spread, and regulation.
A responsible evaluation matches evidence to claim and identifies who benefits, who bears risk, and what monitoring can trigger revision.

conceptMap.title: Recombinant-DNA workflow

I can compare DNA profiles probabilistically without saying a match proves identity or relationship by itself.

sections.label: Molecular tools
sections.title: Different methods produce different evidence
paragraphs: PCR amplifies selected regions, gel or capillary electrophoresis separates fragments, and sequencing identifies nucleotide order. STR markers can support identity comparisons, SNPs can support selected trait or ancestry models, and mitochondrial or Y-chromosome markers follow particular inheritance routes.
A method’s resolution, error rate, target, reference database, and sample quality define what it can support.

sections.label: Profiles and relationships
sections.title: Shared alleles change probability, not certainty
paragraphs: A DNA profile is compared across multiple markers. A match is evaluated against how common the pattern is in a relevant population and against related-source alternatives. Relationship testing calculates likelihood under stated family models. Identical twins, close relatives, mutation, sample mixture, and incomplete data can alter interpretation.
Say that evidence supports one hypothesis more than another; avoid “100 percent proof” when the statistic and alternatives do not justify it.

sections.label: Biotechnology applications
sections.title: DNA evidence can support diagnosis, treatment, ancestry, conservation, and research
paragraphs: Sequencing and marker data can identify variants, track inheritance, characterize organisms, monitor populations, or guide selected therapies. Validity and utility differ by application. An ancestry estimate depends on reference populations and model assumptions; it is not a complete record of culture, nation, kinship, or identity.
Clinical and identity claims need fit-for-purpose validation and professional context.

sections.label: Rights and governance
sections.title: Genetic data affects more than one person
paragraphs: DNA data can reveal health risk, biological relationships, ancestry signals, and information about relatives. Consent, secondary use, security, law enforcement access, discrimination, benefit sharing, patent or ownership claims, community governance, and Indigenous data sovereignty require explicit attention.
Technical capability does not create automatic permission. A responsible decision defines who controls data, how withdrawal works, and how benefits and harms are monitored.

sections.label: Question and model
sections.title: A good investigation connects mechanism to a measurable prediction
paragraphs: Begin with an observation and ask a question narrow enough to test. Identify independent and dependent variables, constants, sample or model population, and the genetic mechanism. Choose a chromosome, inheritance, molecular, or population model because its assumptions fit the question.
A hypothesis should predict a direction or pattern and explain why, not merely state that two variables are related.

sections.label: Method and controls
sections.title: Procedures must make comparisons interpretable
paragraphs: Define sampling, replication, measurement, classification, and data-recording rules before inspecting outcomes. Positive controls show a method can detect an expected result; negative controls reveal contamination or background. Blinding or randomized order can reduce observer and sequence bias when appropriate.
Use safe simulations or supplied data rather than biological samples from learners. Never collect family medical or DNA information.

sections.label: Analysis
sections.title: Calculations must remain traceable to raw evidence
paragraphs: Show counts, units, probability rules, expected values, graph scales, uncertainty, and any exclusions. Compare observed evidence with the selected model and at least one alternative. Statistical output should be interpreted in biological context rather than treated as an automatic truth label.
A significant difference does not measure practical importance or prove a mechanism; a non-significant result does not prove no effect.

sections.label: Communication and revision
sections.title: Reproducibility includes transparent limitations
paragraphs: A complete report links question, method, evidence, reasoning, conclusion, safety, ethics, and limitations. Distinguish planned from exploratory analysis. State which result would make the conclusion stronger, weaker, or require a different model. Peer or teacher feedback should improve traceability rather than reward certainty.
Sharing a method is not permission to share identifiable genetic data. Governance and consent remain part of scientific quality.

sections.label: Evidence architecture
sections.title: Every result belongs to a scale and method
paragraphs: An integrated case can include karyotype, pedigree, cross, recombination, sequence, transcript, protein, cell phenotype, and population data. Record each observation with method, sample, units, time, quality, and scale. Separate direct evidence from calculated values and inferred mechanisms.
A finding at one scale does not automatically establish every later effect. Build the chain explicitly.

sections.label: Model comparison
sections.title: Different mechanisms can predict overlapping evidence
paragraphs: A phenotype could reflect chromosome number, one locus, many loci, regulatory sequence, splicing, protein function, environment, or interaction. Discriminating evidence should differ between explanations, such as segregation pattern, transcript consequence, functional rescue, or matched control.

sections.label: Probability and uncertainty
sections.title: Genetic explanations remain probabilistic
paragraphs: Punnett squares, likelihood ratios, recombination frequencies, penetrance, polygenic scores, and assay errors quantify different uncertainties. Report the denominator and reference. Do not combine percentages from unrelated models or replace an individual decision with a population average.
A precise number can still be biased, poorly calibrated, or irrelevant to the decision at hand.

sections.label: Rights and communication
sections.title: A complete answer includes governance
paragraphs: Genetic evidence can affect relatives and communities. A final recommendation should concern further evidence, counselling, monitoring, or governance—not diagnosis or treatment from a classroom case. Include consent, privacy, access, equity, cultural context, data sovereignty, and who can revise the decision.
Scientific strength is shown by traceability, mechanism, alternatives, and respectful limits, not by eliminating all uncertainty.

D.learningIntention: I am learning to describe a population as a gene pool and explain what genetic equilibrium would require.
successCriteria: I can distinguish an individual genotype from population allele frequencies.
I can calculate an allele frequency from counted alleles.
I can explain why equilibrium is a comparison model rather than a claim that populations never change.
D.materials: Calculator, paper or the Investigation Notebook, and the supplied beetle gene-pool table.
D.safety: This lesson uses synthetic instructional data. It makes no claims about the genetics, health, or identity of any learner or real community.

warmup.title: From organisms to alleles
warmup.prompt: A population contains ten diploid beetles. How many copies of one autosomal gene are represented, and why is that number different from the number of beetles?
warmup.placeholder: State the allele-copy count and explain your reasoning.

sections.label: Scale of analysis
sections.title: A population is more than a head count
paragraphs: A population is a group of individuals of the same species living in the same area at the same time with a realistic opportunity to reproduce. Population genetics changes the question from “What genotype does this organism have?” to “How common is each allele in the breeding population?” That shift matters because evolution is measured as a change in allele frequencies across generations. An individual can develop, acclimate, or move, but an individual does not evolve genetically during its lifetime.

The gene pool is the complete collection of alleles in that population. For a diploid autosomal locus, every individual contributes two allele copies. A population of 100 diploid organisms therefore contains 200 allele copies at that locus, even if only two allele forms—A and a—are present. Frequency is a proportion, so the frequency of A plus the frequency of a equals 1. Symbols p and q are labels for those frequencies, not labels for “strong” and “weak” alleles.

sections.label: Counting evidence
sections.title: Move from genotype counts to allele frequencies
paragraphs: Suppose a synthetic beetle population contains 36 AA individuals, 48 Aa individuals, and 16 aa individuals. There are 200 allele copies. The AA group contributes 72 A alleles, and the heterozygous group contributes 48 more, for 120 A alleles. Therefore p = 120/200 = 0.60. The remaining 80 copies are a, so q = 0.40. Checking p + q = 1 catches many arithmetic errors before they affect later conclusions.

Genotype frequency uses individuals as the denominator: 36/100 = 0.36 for AA, 48/100 = 0.48 for Aa, and 16/100 = 0.16 for aa. Allele frequency uses allele copies as the denominator. Confusing these denominators is the most common conceptual error in this unit. Keep a two-row evidence table—genotypes first, allele contributions second—so every calculated value can be traced back to an observed count.

sections.label: Model baseline
sections.title: What genetic equilibrium means
paragraphs: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes a population in which allele and genotype frequencies remain stable from one generation to the next under a specific set of assumptions. The model imagines a very large, randomly mating population with no mutation, migration, or differential reproductive success among genotypes. Those conditions isolate inheritance from evolutionary forces. If allele frequencies remain constant under the model, ordinary Mendelian segregation by itself does not cause evolution.

Real populations rarely satisfy every assumption perfectly. That is the model’s value, not its failure. Scientists compare observed evidence with the equilibrium prediction, then ask which violated assumption could explain a meaningful departure. A difference does not automatically identify the cause: sampling error, population structure, non-random mating, migration, selection, mutation, or drift may produce different patterns. The model starts an investigation; it does not finish one.

sections.label: Scientific reasoning
sections.title: Use an equilibrium claim carefully
paragraphs: A defensible claim names the population, locus, time interval, and evidence. “This species is in equilibrium” is too broad. A stronger statement is: “At locus R in this sampled population, observed genotype frequencies do not differ meaningfully from the Hardy-Weinberg expectation in this generation.” Even that statement is provisional because one sample can miss rare alleles or local subpopulations. Repeated samples and transparent methods make the inference stronger.

The social context also matters. Allele frequencies describe populations, not the worth, ability, or identity of individuals. Genetic categories can be misused when variation within groups is ignored or when socially defined groups are treated as fixed biological populations. In this course, population-genetic models are used to explain inheritance and evolutionary change. They are not tools for ranking people or making unsupported claims about complex human traits.

sections.label: Assumption set
sections.title: Hold evolutionary forces still
paragraphs: The Hardy-Weinberg model holds five influences still: mutation is absent, migration does not move alleles in or out, mating is random with respect to the locus, the population is effectively very large, and all genotypes have equal reproductive success. Mendelian segregation and random fertilization continue. Under those conditions, allele frequencies remain constant, and expected genotype frequencies can be calculated from p and q after one generation of random mating.

Each assumption points to a real process. Mutation creates new allele forms. Gene flow transports alleles among populations. Non-random mating changes which gametes combine, often changing genotype proportions before it changes allele frequencies. Finite population size allows random sampling error, called genetic drift. Natural or sexual selection creates differences in survival or reproductive contribution. Naming the biological process is more useful than memorizing a list detached from evidence.

sections.label: Prediction
sections.title: Different violations leave different clues
paragraphs: If a storm randomly leaves only a few survivors, allele frequencies may jump unpredictably, especially for rare alleles. If migrants arrive with a different allele distribution, the recipient population should shift toward the migrants’ frequencies. If one genotype leaves more surviving offspring, its associated alleles may increase in a directional pattern. If relatives mate more often than expected, homozygous genotypes may become more frequent while allele frequencies initially remain similar.

These are predictions, not automatic diagnoses. A heterozygote deficit could reflect inbreeding, assortative mating, selection against heterozygotes, genotyping error, or the accidental mixing of two subpopulations in one sample. Scientists use additional evidence—movement records, survival data, parentage, spatial sampling, or repeated generations—to distinguish among explanations. A good investigation is designed around alternatives rather than a single favoured story.

table.caption: Assumptions and evidence that could challenge them
rows: Survival and offspring counts by genotype

sections.label: Testing
sections.title: Observed versus expected is a statistical question
paragraphs: After calculating p and q from the observed sample, scientists calculate expected genotype proportions p², 2pq, and q². Multiplying each proportion by sample size produces expected counts. The differences between observed and expected counts can then be evaluated. Small differences are inevitable because samples are finite. A statistical goodness-of-fit test can help judge whether the discrepancy is larger than expected from sampling alone, provided its assumptions are met.

This course emphasizes the reasoning before formal statistics: define categories, verify totals, calculate an expectation from observed allele frequencies, compare all genotype classes, and examine sample size. A visual difference is not automatically biologically important, and a non-significant result is not proof of perfect equilibrium. Measurement quality and statistical power affect what the evidence can reveal.

sections.label: Model limits
sections.title: Equilibrium is locus-specific and time-specific
paragraphs: One population may appear near equilibrium at one locus while another locus changes under selection. A population may also match expectations this year and depart after migration or an environmental shift. The model therefore applies to a defined locus, population, and generation. Broad claims about an entire species erase variation in geography, time, and selection pressure and should be rejected unless evidence truly supports that scale.

The strongest conclusion combines calculation and uncertainty: state the observed departure, identify plausible mechanisms, and specify the next evidence needed. For example, an unexpected increase in a coastal allele after a shipping route opens is consistent with gene flow, but migration data and comparison populations are needed. “Consistent with” is accurate scientific language when multiple explanations remain possible.

warmup.placeholder: Label every term before doing any arithmetic.

sections.label: Equation meaning
sections.title: Two equations answer different questions
paragraphs: The equation p + q = 1 describes two allele frequencies at one locus: p is the frequency of one allele and q is the frequency of the other. The expanded equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1 describes expected genotype frequencies after random mating: p² for one homozygote, 2pq for heterozygotes, and q² for the other homozygote. The squared terms are not allele counts; they are probabilities that two gametes contribute the same allele.

Before calculating, translate the evidence into a known quantity. A count of individuals with a recessive phenotype can represent q² only when the trait is fully penetrant, the phenotype corresponds uniquely to the homozygous recessive genotype, and the equilibrium model is being used. A direct genotype table allows p and q to be calculated by allele counting and is usually stronger evidence than inferring genotype from phenotype.

sections.label: Worked method
sections.title: Start with the quantity you actually know
paragraphs: In a synthetic population of 1,000 plants, 90 show a recessive phenotype. Under the stated simple model, q² = 90/1,000 = 0.09. Taking the square root gives q = 0.30, so p = 1 − 0.30 = 0.70. Expected heterozygotes are 2pq = 2(0.70)(0.30) = 0.42, or about 420 plants. Expected homozygous dominant individuals are p² = 0.49, or about 490 plants.

A common error is treating 0.09 as q rather than q². That mistake produces q = 0.09, p = 0.91, and a heterozygote estimate that does not follow from the observed recessive genotype frequency. Write the symbol beside every observed value before substituting. Keep frequencies as decimals during calculations, then convert to counts or percentages only when the question requires them.

sections.label: Verification
sections.title: Use three independent checks
paragraphs: First, p and q must each lie from 0 to 1 and must sum to 1. Second, p², 2pq, and q² must also lie from 0 to 1 and sum to 1 within rounding tolerance. Third, expected counts should sum to the sample size. These checks cannot prove the biological assumptions, but they can expose misplaced square roots, omitted factors of two, percentage-decimal errors, and rounding drift.

Keep extra digits until the end. If q² = 17/240, rounding q too early can shift all expected counts. Report a sensible precision that reflects sample size. A calculated frequency such as 0.26643 should not be presented as though five decimal places are biologically exact when the source sample contains only 240 individuals. Precision is part of scientific communication, not cosmetic formatting.

sections.label: Interpretation
sections.title: A correct number still needs a biological sentence
paragraphs: If 2pq = 0.42, write “Under the stated Hardy-Weinberg model, the expected heterozygote frequency is 0.42.” Do not write “42 percent of the population definitely carries the allele” unless the model assumptions and trait relationship justify that inference. The word expected signals that the value comes from a model. Observed genotype counts may differ, and carrier language applies only in an appropriate inheritance context.

When comparing generations, calculate frequencies using each generation’s denominator rather than raw counts. A population can double in size while an allele frequency stays constant, or shrink while an allele frequency changes. Evolutionary change concerns relative allele representation. Population size affects drift and uncertainty, but population growth alone does not tell you the direction of allele-frequency change.

warmup.placeholder: Name at least two mechanisms that could produce the same direction of change.

sections.label: Sources of variation
sections.title: Mutation creates; recombination reshuffles
paragraphs: Mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles because it changes DNA sequence. Most mutations are neutral or harmful in a given context, and a beneficial effect depends on environment and phenotype. Mutation rates at one locus are usually too low to cause rapid population-wide change by themselves, but mutation supplies the variation on which other forces act. Recombination, independent assortment, and fertilization create new allele combinations without creating new alleles.

A mutation enters a gene pool only if it occurs in a lineage that contributes to the next generation. In sexually reproducing organisms, a mutation in a body cell can affect that organism but is not ordinarily inherited. A mutation in a cell lineage producing gametes may be transmitted. Even then, its fate depends on chance, selection, mating, and population structure. Novel does not mean useful, and common does not mean superior.

sections.label: Movement and chance
sections.title: Gene flow and genetic drift change representation
paragraphs: Gene flow occurs when migrants or their gametes reproduce in another population. It can introduce alleles, raise or lower existing frequencies, and often reduce differences between connected populations. The effect depends on the migrants’ allele frequencies, their number relative to residents, and their reproductive contribution. Movement alone is not enough; alleles must enter the recipient gene pool to count as gene flow.

Genetic drift is random change caused by finite sampling from one generation to the next. Its effect is strongest in small populations. A bottleneck sharply reduces population size, while a founder event begins a population from a small, unrepresentative sample. Both can reduce diversity or make rare alleles common by chance. Drift has no goal and does not consistently favour adaptations, although its results can interact with later selection.

sections.label: Differential reproduction
sections.title: Selection links phenotype, environment, and fitness
paragraphs: Natural selection occurs when heritable phenotypic differences lead to differences in survival or reproductive contribution in a particular environment. Fitness is relative reproductive success, not strength, health, or moral value. If an allele contributes to a phenotype that leaves more viable offspring under current conditions, that allele may rise. If conditions change, the direction or strength of selection can also change.

Selection can be directional, stabilizing, disruptive, frequency-dependent, or balanced by trade-offs. A simple rise in one allele is consistent with directional selection but does not prove it. Scientists look for genotype-linked survival, fecundity, or mating differences and compare populations or years with different conditions. Selection acts on phenotypes, while evolution is recorded as changing genetic composition in the population.

table.caption: Mechanism signatures and cautions
rows: Movement without reproduction is not gene flow
Replicates change unpredictably; small populations vary most
A single direction is not expected across replicates
Frequency change alone does not prove selection
Usually a slow direct effect at one locus

sections.label: Evidence integration
sections.title: Separate mechanism, pattern, and claim
paragraphs: A pattern is what the data show: an allele rose, diversity fell, populations became more similar, or replicate populations diverged. A mechanism is the process proposed to produce the pattern. A claim connects the two and must be supported by evidence beyond the pattern when alternatives exist. For example, convergence after a migration corridor opens supports gene flow more strongly when tagged migrants reproduce and carry the changing allele.

Non-random mating deserves careful placement. It directly changes genotype combinations and can increase homozygosity, but it does not necessarily change allele frequencies by itself. Sexual selection can change allele frequencies when mating differences lead to unequal reproductive success. Clear language prevents the false shortcut that every departure from random mating is automatically allele-frequency evolution in one generation.

warmup.title: Who is affected?
warmup.prompt: A flowering plant gains pollination while an insect gains food. What evidence is needed before calling the interaction mutualism?
warmup.placeholder: Describe a measurable benefit for each population.

sections.label: Ecological scale
sections.title: Populations meet in communities
paragraphs: A community includes the populations of different species living and interacting in an area. An ecosystem includes that community plus non-living conditions and transfers of energy and matter. These levels answer different questions. Population data describe abundance or genetic change within one species; community data describe interactions, diversity, and composition among species; ecosystem data add factors such as temperature, water, nutrients, disturbance, and productivity.

Interactions can alter survival, growth, or reproduction and therefore change abundance and selection pressure. Their effects are often represented as positive, negative, or approximately neutral for each participant. This notation is a starting framework: +/+ for mutualism, +/− for predation, herbivory, or parasitism, −/− for competition, and +/0 for commensalism. The symbols refer to measured effects relative to an appropriate comparison, not intention or moral value.

sections.label: Classification
sections.title: Use outcomes, not appearances
paragraphs: In mutualism, both populations receive a net benefit, but the relationship may be obligate or optional and may shift with conditions. In commensalism, one benefits while the other has no detected effect. Demonstrating a true zero effect is difficult because an unmeasured cost or benefit may exist. Parasitism benefits a parasite while reducing host fitness, usually without immediately killing the host. Predation consumes another organism, while herbivory consumes plant or algal tissue and may or may not kill the organism.

Competition occurs when organisms use a resource that is limiting. Intraspecific competition occurs within a species; interspecific competition occurs between species. The presence of two species near the same resource does not prove competition. Evidence could include reduced growth when they co-occur, resource overlap, removal experiments, or shifts in resource use. A classification is strongest when it identifies the resource and measures effects on both populations.

table.caption: Interaction effects and evidence
rows: Reproductive or survival benefit to both
A shared limiting resource and reduced performance
Consumer gain and prey or host cost
Benefit to one; no detected effect on the other

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Interactions are not fixed personality traits
paragraphs: A plant-mycorrhizal association may be mutually beneficial when soil nutrients are scarce, yet the carbon cost to the plant may exceed nutrient benefit under other conditions. A normally commensal microorganism may become harmful when host defences or location change. Competition can be weak when resources are abundant and strong during drought. Therefore, interaction labels summarize evidence under stated conditions rather than permanently defining the species involved.

Direct and indirect effects also differ. A predator directly lowers prey survival but may indirectly release a plant from herbivory. Removing one competitor can increase another species, which then changes a third interaction. Community ecology follows these pathways without assuming every correlation is direct. Experimental controls, time series, and food-web context help identify whether an observed response is caused by the focal interaction.

sections.label: Investigation
sections.title: Build a fair interaction claim
paragraphs: A useful investigation defines the response variable for each participant. For pollination, flower visits alone show contact but not necessarily benefit. Researchers may compare seed set in accessible and excluded flowers while also measuring pollinator food collection or reproductive success. For competition, compare performance alone and together while controlling total density, resource level, and starting size. Replication helps separate an interaction effect from individual variation.

Observational evidence can still be valuable when experiments would be unethical or impractical. A time series may show predator abundance preceding changes in prey abundance, or long-term monitoring may reveal plant recruitment after pollinator decline. The claim should remain proportional: association supports a hypothesis, while manipulative or converging evidence may strengthen causal inference. Always report the spatial and temporal scale because effects can reverse across scales.

conceptMap.title: Community interaction evidence
conceptMap.description: Identify participants, measure effects on each, and interpret the relationship within its ecological context.

nodes.label: Effects

interaction.title: Species-interaction model
interaction.intro: Each case includes an observation and a stronger comparison. Classify only after considering both participants.
interaction.prompt: Choose a case and decide which evidence justifies the interaction label.

cases.label: Flower and pollinator
cases.evidence: Excluding visits lowers seed set; insects gain measurable food and produce more offspring where flowers are available.
cases.explanation: Both populations show a fitness-related benefit under these conditions, supporting mutualism.

cases.label: Epiphyte and tree
cases.evidence: The epiphyte gains light and support; tree growth and reproduction do not differ within measurement limits.
cases.explanation: The evidence supports commensalism provisionally, while acknowledging that a small tree effect may be undetected.

cases.label: Two seed consumers

successCriteria: I can connect defence or resource-use traits to costs and benefits.
I can interpret predator-prey patterns without assuming a simple one-way cause.
